They say that one needs faith in order to renounce everything; indeed, one hears something even stranger — that a person complains that he has lost his faith, and when one looks at the scale to see where he is, one sees, oddly enough, that he has only reached the point at which he is to make the infinite movement of resignation. By resignation I renounce everything; this movement I make by myself, and when I do not make it, it is because I am cowardly and soft and without enthusiasm, and do not feel the meaning of the high dignity to which every human being is appointed: to be his own censor — which is far more distinguished than being censor general for the whole Roman republic. This movement I make by myself, and what I gain by it is myself in my eternal consciousness, in blessed agreement with my love for the eternal Being. By faith I renounce nothing; on the contrary, by faith I receive everything, precisely in the sense in which it is said that he who has faith like a mustard seed can move mountains. A purely human courage is required to renounce all temporality in order to gain eternity; but this I do gain, and in all eternity I cannot renounce it — that would be a self-contradiction. But a paradoxical and humble courage is required to grasp the whole of temporality by virtue of the absurd; and this courage is faith's. By faith Abraham did not renounce Isaac; by faith Abraham received Isaac. By virtue of resignation that rich young man should have given everything away; but when he had done so, the knight of faith should have said to him: by virtue of the absurd you shall receive every penny back, can you believe this? And this saying should by no means be a matter of indifference to the formerly rich young man; for if he gave away his goods because he was tired of them, then his resignation is in poor shape.

4.31.oldText: Temporality, finitude — that is what everything turns on. By my own strength I can resign everything, and then find peace and rest in the pain; I can put up with anything, even if that dreadful demon, more terrifying than the skeleton-man who frightens people, even if madness held up the fool's costume before my eyes, and I understood from its expression that it was I who was to put it on — I can still save my soul, so long as it matters more to me that my love for God conquer in me than my earthly happiness. A person can, even in this last moment, gather his whole soul into one single glance toward the heaven from which every good gift comes, and this glance shall be intelligible to him and to the one whom it seeks: that he was nevertheless faithful to his love. Then he shall calmly put on the costume. He whose soul has not this romance has sold his soul, whether he got a kingdom for it or a wretched silver coin. But by my own strength I cannot get the least of what belongs to finitude; for I constantly use my strength to resign everything. By my own strength I can give up the princess, and I shall not become some sour-faced creature, but find joy and peace and rest in my pain; but by my own strength I cannot get her back, for I use my strength precisely to resign. By faith, however — says that wondrous knight — by faith you shall receive her by virtue of the absurd.

4.32.oldText: You see, this movement I cannot make. As soon as I try to begin it, everything turns around, and I flee back into the pain of resignation. I can swim in

4.33.oldText: life, but for this mystical hovering I am too heavy. To exist in such a way that my opposition to existence at every moment expresses itself as the most beautiful and certain harmony with it — that I cannot do. And yet it must be glorious to get the princess, that I say at every moment; and the knight of resignation who does not say it is a fraud — he has not had a single wish, and he has not kept the wish young in his pain. Perhaps there was someone who found it convenient enough that the wish was no longer alive, that the arrow of pain was blunted; but such a person is no knight. A free-born soul who caught himself in this would despise himself and begin afresh, and above all, would not allow his soul to be deceived by itself. And yet it must be glorious to get the princess, and yet the knight of faith is the only happy one, the heir of finitude, while the knight of resignation is a stranger and an alien. So to get the princess, to live joyfully and happily with her day in and day out — for this too is conceivable, that the knight of resignation might get the princess, but his soul would have seen through the impossibility of their future happiness — so to live joyfully and happily every moment by virtue of the absurd, every moment to see the sword hovering over the head of the beloved, and yet not to find rest in the pain of resignation, but joy by virtue of the absurd — that is wondrous. He who does this is great, the only great one. The thought of it moves my soul, which was never stingy in admiring greatness.

4.34.oldText: If now everyone in my generation who will not stop at faith really is a man who has grasped the horror of life, who has understood what Daub means when he says that a soldier who alone stands sentry with a loaded musket by a powder magazine on a stormy night gets strange thoughts; if now everyone who will not stop at faith really is a man who had soul-strength to grasp it and then took the time to become alone with the thought that the wish was an impossibility; if everyone who will not stop at faith is a man who in pain was reconciled and was reconciled by the pain; if everyone who will not stop at faith is a man who next (and if he has not done all the foregoing, then he should not bother himself when faith is in question) did the wondrous, grasped the whole of existence by virtue of the absurd — then what I write is the highest eulogy of my generation, by the lowliest in it, who could only make the movement of resignation. But why then will people not stop at it? Why does one sometimes hear that people are ashamed to confess that they have faith? This I cannot grasp. If I should ever come to the point of being able to make this movement, then in the future I will drive with four horses.

4.35.oldText: Is it really so? All this philistinism that I see in life — and which I let my deeds, not my words, judge — is it really not what it seems; is it the wonder? It would be conceivable; for that hero of faith bore a striking resemblance to it, since that hero of faith was not even an ironist or a humorist, but something even higher. Much is said in our age about irony and humor, especially by people who have never managed to practice them, but who nevertheless know how to explain everything. I am not entirely unacquainted with these two passions; I know a little more about them than what stands in German and German-Danish handbooks. I know therefore that these two passions are essentially different from the passion of faith. Irony and humor also reflect upon themselves, and so belong to the sphere of infinite resignation; their elasticity lies in the fact that the individual is incommensurable with actuality.

4.36.oldText: The last movement, the paradoxical movement of faith, I cannot make, be it duty or whatever, although I would like to do so, more gladly than gladly. Whether a person has the right to say this must be left to him; it becomes a matter between him and the eternal Being, who is the object of faith, whether he can in this respect reach an amicable understanding. What every person can do is this: he can make the movement of infinite resignation; and I, for my part, would not hesitate to declare cowardly anyone who would imagine he cannot do it. With faith it is another matter. But what no person has the right to do is to make others believe that faith is something insignificant, or that it is an easy matter, when it is the greatest and the hardest.

4.37.oldText: The story of Abraham is grasped in another way. People praise God's grace, that he gave him Isaac back; the whole thing was only a trial. A trial — this word can say much and little, and yet the whole thing is over as quickly as it is said. One mounts a winged horse; in the same instant one is on Mount Moriah; in the same instant one sees the ram; one forgets that Abraham only rode on an ass, which goes slowly along the way, that he had a three-day journey, that he needed some time to split the wood, to bind Isaac, and to whet the knife.

4.38.oldText: And yet people praise Abraham. The one who is to give the speech can sleep right up to the last quarter-hour before he speaks; the listener can fall asleep during the speech; for everything goes easily enough, with no inconvenience to either side. If a man were present who suffered from sleeplessness, then perhaps he would go home, sit down in a corner, and think: it is the matter of a moment, the whole thing — only wait a minute, and you see the ram, and the trial is over. If the speaker met him in this state, then I think he would step before him in all his dignity and say: ‘Wretched man, that you can let your soul sink into such folly; no miracle takes place, and the whole of life is a trial.' As the speaker pressed on in his outpouring, he became more and more excited, more and more pleased with himself; and while he had noticed no congestion of blood when he was speaking about Abraham, he now felt the vein swelling on his forehead. Perhaps he would lose nose and mouth if the sinner answered calmly and with dignity: But that is what you preached about last Sunday.

4.39.oldText: Then let us either draw a line through Abraham, or let us learn to be terrified at the enormous paradox that is the meaning of his life — that we may understand that our age, like every age, can be glad if it has faith. If Abraham is not a nullity, a phantom, a piece of finery used to pass the time, then the fault can never lie in the fact that the sinner wished to do likewise, but it is essential to see how great was what Abraham did, so that the man may judge for himself whether he has the calling and the courage to be tried in such a thing. The comic contradiction in the speaker's behavior was that he made Abraham into an insignificance, and yet would forbid the other to behave in the same way.

4.40.oldText: Should one then not dare to speak of Abraham? I think one may indeed. If I were to speak about him, I would first describe the pain of the trial. To this end I would, like a leech, suck all the anxiety and need and torment out of a father's suffering, in order to be able to describe what Abraham suffered, while nevertheless under all this he believed. I would remind people that the journey lasted three days and a good portion of the fourth — yes, these three and a half days were to become infinitely much longer than the few thousand years that separate me from Abraham. Then I would remind people that, in my opinion, every person may still turn back before he begins on such a thing, and at every moment can repent and turn back. If one does this, then I fear no danger; nor do I fear that I shall awaken in people a desire to be tried in the manner of Abraham. But if one wants to put on the market a cheap edition of Abraham, and yet forbid everyone to do as he did, then it is ridiculous.

4.41.oldText: It is therefore now my intention to draw out from the story of Abraham, in the form of *Problemata*, the dialectical that lies in it, in order to see what an enormous paradox faith is — a paradox capable of making a murder into a holy and God-pleasing act, a paradox that gives Abraham Isaac back, which no thinking can master, since faith begins precisely where thinking leaves off.

5.0.oldText: The ethical as such is the universal, and as the universal it is what holds for everyone, which from another side may be expressed thus: that it holds at every moment. It rests immanent in itself, has nothing outside itself that is its *telos*, but is itself the *telos* for everything that has it outside itself; and once the ethical has taken this into itself, it goes no further. Determined as immediate sensuous and psychic being, the single individual is the single individual who has his *telos* in the universal, and this is his ethical task: continually to express himself in this, to annul his singularity in order to become the universal. As soon as the single individual would assert himself in his singularity over against the universal, he sins, and only by acknowledging this can he be reconciled again with the universal. Every time the single individual, after having entered into the universal, feels an impulse to assert himself as the single individual, he is in temptation, out of which he works himself only by repenting and giving up himself as the single individual into the universal. If this is the highest that can be said about a human being and his existence, then the ethical has the same character as a person's eternal blessedness, which through all eternity and at every moment is his *telos*, since it would be a contradiction that it could be given up (i.e., teleologically suspended), since it, as soon as it is suspended, is forfeited; while what is suspended is not forfeited, but precisely preserved in the higher, which is its *telos*.

5.1.oldText: If this is the case, then Hegel is right when he allows a human being in the good and in conscience to be determined only as the single individual; he is right to regard this character as a ‘moral form of evil' (cf. especially the *Philosophy of Right*), which must be annulled in the teleology of the ethical, so that the single individual who remains in this stage either sins or lies in temptation. What Hegel is *not* right about, however, is to speak about faith, not right in not protesting loudly and audibly when Abraham is given honor and glory as a father of faith, while he ought rather to be shown the door and expelled as a murderer.

5.2.oldText: For faith is precisely this paradox: that the single individual is higher than the universal, yet, mark well, in such a way that the movement repeats itself — that is, that having been in the universal, he now, as the single individual, isolates himself as higher than the universal. If this is not faith, then Abraham is lost; then faith has never existed in the world, precisely because it has always existed. For if the ethical, i.e., the moral, is the highest, and there is nothing incommensurable left in a person except in such a way that this incommensurable is evil, i.e., the singular which is to be expressed in the universal, then one needs no other categories than those Greek philosophy possessed, or those that can be drawn out of these by consistent thinking. This Hegel ought not to have concealed; for he had, after all, Greek studies behind him.

5.3.oldText: One often hears men who, lacking immersion in studies, immerse themselves instead in phrases, declare that a light shines over the Christian world, while a darkness broods over heathenism. This kind of talk has always seemed to me strange, since to this day every more thorough thinker, every more serious artist, rejuvenates himself in the eternal youth of the Greek people. Such an utterance can be explained by the fact that one does not know what to say, but only that one must say something. It is in order to say that heathenism did not have faith; but if by this one is to have said something, one must be a little clearer about what one understands by faith — otherwise one sinks back into such phrases. To explain the whole of existence, faith included, without having any conception of what faith is, is easy; and the man who calculates on admiration is no worst calculator in life when he has such an explanation in hand — for it is as Boileau says: *un sot trouve toujours un plus sot, qui l'admire*.

5.4.oldText: Faith is precisely this paradox: that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal, is justified over against it, not subordinate but superior — yet, mark well, in such a way that it is the single individual who, having been as the single individual subordinate to the universal, now through the universal becomes the single individual who, as the single individual, is superior to it; that the single individual as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute. This standpoint cannot be mediated; for all mediation takes place precisely by virtue of the universal; it is and remains in all eternity a paradox, inaccessible to thought. And yet faith is this paradox; or else (these are the consequences which I would beg the reader to keep *in mente* at every point, even though it would be too cumbersome for me to write them out everywhere), or else there has never been faith, precisely because it has always been; or else Abraham is lost.

5.5.oldText: That this paradox can easily be confused, for the single individual, with a temptation, is true enough; but for that reason one ought not to conceal it. That the entire constitution of many a person may be such that it repels them is true enough; but for that reason one ought not to make faith into something else in order to be able to have it too — but rather confess that one does not have it; while those who do have faith ought to set themselves the task of putting forward some marks by which one can distinguish the paradox from a temptation.

5.6.oldText: Now the story of Abraham contains just such a teleological suspension of the ethical. There has been no lack of clever heads and thorough scholars who have found analogies to it. Their wisdom amounts to the fine proposition that fundamentally everything is the same. If one will look a little more closely, I very much doubt that one will find a single analogy in the whole world, except a later one, which proves nothing, when it stands fast that Abraham represents faith, and that it is normally expressed in him, whose life is not only the most paradoxical conceivable, but so paradoxical that it cannot be thought at all. He acts by virtue of the absurd; for it is precisely the absurd that he, as the single individual, is higher than the universal. This paradox cannot be mediated; for as soon as he begins to do so, he must confess that he was in a temptation; and if so, he never gets to sacrifice Isaac; or if he has sacrificed Isaac, he must, repenting, return back to the universal. By virtue of the absurd he gets Isaac back again. Abraham, therefore, is at no moment a tragic hero, but something quite different — either a murderer or a believer. The mediating term that saves the tragic hero is what Abraham does not have. Therefore it is that I can understand a tragic hero, but cannot understand Abraham, even if in a certain demented way I admire him more than all others.

5.7.oldText: Abraham's relation to Isaac, ethically expressed, is quite simply this: that the father shall love the son higher than himself. But the ethical has within its own compass several gradations; we shall see whether in this story there is to be found any such higher expression of the ethical that can ethically explain his behavior, can ethically justify his suspending the ethical obligation toward the son, without therefore moving outside the teleology of the ethical.

5.8.oldText: When an undertaking that is the concern of an entire people is hindered, when such an enterprise is halted by heaven's disfavor, when the angry deity sends a calm that mocks all efforts, when the seer fulfills his heavy task and proclaims that the god demands a young girl as a sacrifice — then the father shall heroically bring this sacrifice. Magnanimously he shall conceal his pain, even though he might wish himself to be ‘the lowly man who dares to weep,' not the king who must act royally. And though the pain forces its way solitary into his breast, though he has only three confidants among the people, soon the whole people shall be confidants of his pain, but also confidants of his deed — that for the welfare of the whole he was willing to sacrifice her, the daughter, the lovely young girl. *O bosom! O fair cheeks, light yellow hair* (v. 687). And the daughter shall move him by her tears, and the father shall turn his face away, but the hero shall lift the knife. — When the news of this reaches the ancestral home, then the lovely girls of Greece shall blush with enthusiasm, and if the daughter was a bride, then the betrothed shall not be angered, but shall be proud to share in the father's deed, because the girl belonged to him more tenderly than she belonged to the father.

5.9.oldText: When the bold judge who saved Israel in the hour of need, in one breath binds God and himself by the same vow, then he shall heroically transform the young girl's jubilation, the beloved daughter's joy, into sorrow, and all Israel shall mourn with her over her virginal youth; but every free-born man shall understand, every brave woman shall admire Jephthah, and every maiden in Israel shall wish to act as his daughter did. For what good was it that Jephthah won by his vow, if he did not keep it — should not the victory then be taken from the people again?

5.10.oldText: When a son forgets his duty, when the state entrusts the sword of judgment to the father, when the laws demand the punishment from the father's hand, then the father shall heroically forget that the guilty one is his son, he shall magnanimously conceal his pain; but there shall not be a single one among the people, not even the son, who does not admire the father; and every time Rome's laws are interpreted, it shall be remembered that many have interpreted them more learnedly, but none more gloriously than Brutus.

5.11.oldText: If, on the other hand, Agamemnon, while a favorable wind was carrying his fleet under full sail to its goal, had dispatched that messenger to fetch Iphigenia in order to sacrifice her; if Jephthah, without being bound by any vow that decided the people's fate, had said to his daughter: now mourn for two months over your short youth, for I will sacrifice you; if Brutus had had a righteous son and yet had called for the lictors to execute him — who then would have understood them? If these three men, when asked why they had done it, had answered: it is a trial in which we are tested, would one then have understood them better?

5.12.oldText: When Agamemnon, Jephthah, Brutus in the decisive moment heroically overcomes the pain, has heroically lost the beloved and only has yet to complete the deed outwardly, then there shall never be a noble soul in the world who does not have tears of sympathy for their pain, of admiration for their deed. If, on the other hand, these three men in the decisive moment were to add to the heroism with which they bore the pain the little remark: it will not happen, after all — who then would understand them? If they added by way of explanation: this we believe by virtue of the absurd — who then would understand them better? For who would not easily understand that it was absurd? But who would understand that one could then believe it?

5.13.oldText: The difference between the tragic hero and Abraham is easily noticed. The tragic hero still remains within the ethical. He lets one expression of the ethical have its *telos* in a higher expression of the ethical; he reduces the ethical relation between father and son, or daughter and father, to a feeling that has its dialectic in its relation to the idea of moral life. There can therefore be no question here of a teleological suspension of the ethical itself.

5.14.oldText: With Abraham it is otherwise. By his deed he stepped over the entire ethical, and had a higher *telos* outside it, in relation to which he suspended the ethical. For I would still like to know how one would bring Abraham's deed into relation with the universal — whether any contact whatever can be discovered between what Abraham did and the universal, other than that Abraham transgressed it. It is not to save a people, not to uphold the idea of the state, that Abraham does it; not to appease angry gods. If there were any question of the deity being angry, then he was angry only with Abraham, and Abraham's whole deed stands in no relation to the universal — it is a purely private undertaking. Whereas, then, the tragic hero is great by his moral virtue, Abraham is great by a purely personal virtue. There is no higher expression of the ethical in Abraham's life than this: that the father shall love the son. The ethical in the sense of the moral cannot here come into question at all. Insofar as the universal was present, it was hidden in Isaac, hidden, so to speak, in Isaac's loins, and would have to cry out with Isaac's mouth: do not do it, you are annihilating everything.

5.15.oldText: Why does Abraham then do it? For God's sake, and entirely identical with this, for his own sake. For God's sake he does it, because God demands this proof of his faith; for his own sake he does it, that he may furnish the proof. The unity of these is quite correctly expressed in the word with which one has always designated this relationship: it is a trial, a temptation. A temptation; but what does this mean? What otherwise tempts a person is what would hold him back from doing his duty; but here the temptation is the ethical itself, which would hold him back from doing God's will. But what then is duty? Duty, after all, is precisely the expression of God's will.

5.16.oldText: Here the necessity of a new category appears, in order to understand Abraham. Such a relation to the deity heathenism does not know. The tragic hero does not enter into any private relation to the deity; rather, the ethical is the divine, and therefore the paradox in it can be mediated in the universal.

5.17.oldText: Abraham cannot be mediated, which can also be expressed thus: he cannot speak. As soon as I speak, I express the universal; and when I do not, no one can understand me. As soon, then, as Abraham wants to express himself in the universal, he must say that his situation is a temptation; for he has no higher expression of the universal which stands above the universal that he is transgressing.

5.18.oldText: While Abraham, therefore, awakens my admiration, he also terrifies me. The man who denies himself and sacrifices himself for duty gives up the finite in order to grasp the infinite; he is secure enough. The tragic hero gives up the certain for the still more certain, and the spectator's eye rests upon him in security. But the man who gives up the universal in order to grasp something still higher, which is not the universal — what is he doing? Is it possible that this can be anything but a temptation? And if it is possible, but the single individual then made a mistake, what salvation is there for him? He suffers all the pain of the tragic hero; he annihilates his joy in the world; he renounces everything; and perhaps in the same instant he shuts himself off from that exalted joy that was so dear to him that he would buy it at any price. Him the spectator cannot understand at all, nor securely let his eye rest on him. Perhaps it cannot be done at all, what the believer intends, since it is, after all, unthinkable. Or if it could be done, if the single individual had misunderstood the deity — what salvation would there be for him then? The tragic hero needs tears and demands tears; and where was the envious eye so barren that it could not weep with Agamemnon? But where was the man whose soul was so deluded that he presumed to weep over Abraham? The tragic hero completes his deed in a definite moment of time; but in the course of time he does what is no less, he visits the one whose soul is enclosed by sorrow, whose breast cannot get air for stifled sighs, whose thoughts hang upon him heavy, pregnant with tears; he shows himself to him, he lifts the spell of sorrow, he loosens the corset, he draws forth the tear, as the sufferer forgets his sufferings in his. Abraham one cannot weep over. One approaches him with a *horror religiosus*, as Israel approached Mount Sinai. — If, then, the solitary man who climbs Mount Moriah, whose peak rises sky-high above the plains of Aulis — if he is not a sleepwalker who walks securely over the abyss, while the one who stands at the foot of the mountain and looks at it trembles with anxiety, and from reverence and horror does not even dare to call to him — if he becomes confused in himself, if he had made a mistake! — Thanks! again thanks! to the man who reaches out to one whom life's sorrows have attacked and left naked, reaches out to him the expression, the leaf of the word, with which he can hide his wretchedness. Thanks be to you, great Shakespeare, you who can say everything, everything, everything precisely as it is — and yet why did you never utter this torment? Did you perhaps reserve it for yourself? as the beloved whose name one cannot even bear the world to mention; for a poet purchases this power of the word, to utter all the heavy secrets of others, at the price of a little secret he cannot utter; and a poet is not an apostle, he casts out devils only by the power of the devil.

5.19.oldText: But when the ethical is in this way teleologically suspended, how does the single individual exist, in whom it is suspended? He exists as the single individual in opposition to the universal. Does he then sin? For this is the form of sin, viewed in the idea, in such a way that, even though the child does not sin, because it is not conscious of its existence as such, its existence, viewed in the idea, is nevertheless sin, and the ethical demands itself of it at every moment. If one will deny that this form can be repeated in such a way that it is not sin, then judgment is passed on Abraham. How then did Abraham exist? He believed. This is the paradox by which he keeps to the peak, which he cannot make clear to anyone else; for the paradox is that he, as the single individual, places himself in an absolute relation to the absolute. Is he justified? His justification is again the paradox; for if he is, he is not so by virtue of being something universal, but by virtue of being the single individual.

5.20.oldText: How then does the single individual assure himself that he is justified? It is easy enough to level the whole of existence on the idea of the state, or on the idea of society. If one does this, then one can also easily mediate; for then one never comes to the paradox that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal — which I can also expressively put in a saying of Pythagoras: that the odd number is more perfect than the even. Insofar as one occasionally in our age hears an answer in the

5.21.oldText: direction of the paradox, it usually runs thus: it is to be judged by the outcome. A hero who has become a *skandalon* to his contemporaries, in the consciousness that he is a paradox who cannot make himself understood, calls confidently to his contemporaries: the outcome will surely prove that I was right. In our age one hears this call more rarely; for, just as our age does not produce heroes — which is its defect — so it has the good thing about it that it also produces few caricatures. When, then, in our age one hears the words ‘it is to be judged by the outcome,' one is at once clear about whom one has the honor of speaking with. Those who talk like this are a numerous tribe, whom under one common name I will call the Docents. They live, in their thoughts, secured in existence; they have a fixed position and certain prospects in a well-organized state; they have centuries, perhaps even millennia, between themselves and the convulsions of existence; they do not fear that such things can be repeated — what would the police and the newspapers say? Their work in life is to judge the great men, and to judge them by the outcome. Such conduct toward greatness reveals a strange mixture of arrogance and wretchedness — arrogance, because they think themselves called to judge; wretchedness, because they do not feel their lives even remotely related to the lives of the great. Anyone who is even a little *erectioris ingenii* has not yet become an entirely cold and clammy mollusk; and as he draws near to the great, it cannot ever leave his mind that since the creation of the world it has been the custom and use that the outcome comes last, and that, when one is truly to learn anything from the great, one must precisely pay attention to the beginning. If the one who is to act will judge himself by the outcome, then he never gets to begin. Even though the outcome may delight the whole world, that does not help the hero; for the outcome he learned of only when the whole thing was over, and by that he did not become a hero — he was a hero by the fact that he began.

5.22.oldText: Furthermore, the outcome (insofar as it is finitude's answer to the infinite question) is, in its dialectic, entirely incommensurable with the existence of the hero. Or shall it prove that Abraham was justified in relating himself as the single individual to the universal, that by a wonder he received Isaac? If Abraham had really sacrificed Isaac, would he then have been less justified?

5.23.oldText: But people are curious about the outcome, as about the outcome of a book; the anxiety, the need, the paradox they want to know nothing about. They flirt aesthetically with the outcome; it comes just as unexpectedly but also just as easily as a winning lottery ticket; and when they have heard the outcome, they have edified themselves. And yet no temple-robber, working in chains and irons, is so base a criminal as the man who in this way plunders the holy; and yet Judas, who sold his Lord for thirty pieces of silver, is no more contemptible than the man who in this way sells the great.

5.24.oldText: It goes against my soul to speak inhumanly about the great, to let it dim into an enormous distance in indistinct shape, to let it be great without the human element in it being brought out, whereby it ceases to be great; for it is not what happens to me that makes me great, but what I do; and surely no one believes that a man became great because he won the great prize in the lottery. If a person was born in lowly circumstances, I demand of him still that he should not be so inhuman toward himself that he can think of the King's castle only at a distance and dream vaguely of its greatness, and at one and the same time wish to exalt it and to nullify it by exalting it in a base way; I demand of him that he should be man enough to step forward there too with confidence and dignity. He shall not be inhuman enough to want to violate everything by storming into the King's halls straight from the street; by that he loses more than the King. On the contrary, he shall find a joy in observing every command of decorum with cheerful and confident enthusiasm, which will precisely make him bold. This is only an image; for that distinction is only a very imperfect expression for the distance of spirit. I demand of every person that he should not think so inhumanly about himself that he dare not enter those palaces where not merely the memory of the elect dwells, but where they themselves dwell. He shall not impudently push his way in and impose his kinship on them; he shall be blessed every time he bows down before them; but he shall be bold and confident and always be something more than a charwoman; for if he will not be more, then he never gets in. And what shall help him is precisely the anxiety and the need by which the great are tried; for otherwise these would, if he has any marrow in him, only awaken his just envy. And what can only be great at a distance, what one would by means of empty and hollow phrases make into something great — that one annihilates oneself.

5.25.oldText: Who was great in the world like that gracious woman, the mother of God, the Virgin Mary? And yet how does one talk about her? That she was the gracious among women does not make her great; and were it not for the strange fact that those who hear can think just as inhumanly as those who speak, every young girl might surely ask: why was I not also the gracious one? And if I had nothing else to say, I would not at all dismiss such a question as foolish; for in regard to a favor, abstractly viewed, every person has equal right. They leave out the need, the anxiety, the paradox. My thinking is as pure as anyone's, and he who can think such things — his thinking will be pure too, and he also has the dreadful to expect, if it is not so; for he who has once gotten these

5.26.oldText: images before him cannot get rid of them again, and if he sins against them, then they take their revenge dreadfully through silent wrath, more dreadful than the loud voices of ten ravenous reviewers. Mary did indeed bear the child wondrously, but it nevertheless went with her in the way of women; and that time is the time of anxiety, of need, and of the paradox. The angel was indeed a ministering spirit, but he was not an obliging spirit who went to the other young girls of Israel and said: do not despise Mary, the extraordinary is happening to her. But the angel came only to Mary, and no one could understand her. Yet what woman was so violated as Mary, and is it not also true here that the one whom God blesses, He curses in the same breath? This is the spirit's understanding of Mary; and she is by no means — what it offends me to have to say, but offends me still more that people have thoughtlessly and flirtingly understood her so — she is by no means a fine lady sitting decked out and playing with a divine child. When she nevertheless said: behold, I am the handmaid of the Lord — then she is great, and I think it should not be hard to explain why she became the mother of God. She needs no worldly admiration, just as little as Abraham needs tears; for she was not a heroine, and he was not a hero, but they did not become greater than these by being exempted from the need and the torment and the paradox, but became so through these.

5.27.oldText: It is great, when the poet, in setting his tragic hero before the admiration of men, dares to say: weep over him, for he deserves it; for it is great to deserve the tears of those who deserve to shed tears; it is great that the poet dares to keep the crowd in check, dares to chastise people, that everyone test himself whether he is worthy to weep over the hero — for the running spittle of blubberers is a defilement of the holy. — Yet greater than all this is it, that the knight of faith dares to say even to the noble person who would weep over him: weep not for me, but weep for yourself.

5.28.oldText: One is moved; one looks back to those beautiful times; sweet, soft longings lead one to the wished-for goal of seeing Christ walk about in the promised land. One forgets the anxiety, the need, the paradox. Was it so easy a matter not to make a mistake? Was it not dreadful that this man, who walked among the others, was God? Was it not dreadful to sit at table with him? Was it so easy a matter to become an apostle? But the outcome, eighteen centuries — that helps; it helps with this shabby deception by which one deceives oneself and others. I do not feel the courage to wish to be contemporary with such events; but for that reason I do not judge harshly those who made a mistake, nor lightly those who saw what was right.

5.29.oldText: But I return to Abraham. In the time before the outcome, Abraham was either at every minute a murderer, or we stand at the paradox, which is higher than all mediations.

5.30.oldText: Abraham's story therefore contains a teleological suspension of the ethical. As the single individual he became higher than the universal. This is the paradox, which cannot be mediated. It is just as inexplicable how he came into it, as it is inexplicable how he remains in it. If this is not the case with Abraham, then he is not even a tragic hero, but a murderer. To go on calling him father of faith, to talk of this to people who concern themselves with nothing but words, is thoughtless. A tragic hero a person can become by his own powers, but the knight of faith cannot. When a person enters upon the in a certain sense difficult way of the tragic hero, then many can advise him; he who walks the narrow way of faith — no one can advise him, no one can understand him. Faith is a

5.31.oldText: wonder; and yet no person is excluded from it; for that in which all human life is united is in passion, and faith is a passion.

6.0.oldText: The ethical is the universal, and as such, in turn, the divine. One is therefore right to say that every duty is fundamentally a duty toward God; but if one cannot say more, then one is also saying that I have, properly speaking, no duty toward God. Duty becomes duty by being referred to God; but in duty itself I do not enter into relation with God. Thus it is a duty to love one's neighbor. It is a duty insofar as it is referred to God; but in the duty I enter into relation not with God but with the neighbor whom I love. If I say in this connection that it is my duty to love God, then I am really saying only a tautology, insofar as ‘God' is here taken in an entirely abstract sense as the divine, i.e., the universal, i.e., duty. The whole existence of the human race rounds itself off completely as a sphere within itself, and the ethical is at once both that which limits and that which fills out. God becomes an invisible, vanishing point, an impotent thought; his power is only in the ethical, which fills out existence. So insofar as anyone should fall into wanting to love God in any other sense than the one indicated here, then he is overstrained; he loves a phantom which, if it had only enough power to speak, would say to him: I do not demand your love, only stay where you belong. Insofar as anyone should fall into wanting to love God otherwise, then this love becomes suspect, like the love Rousseau speaks of, by which a person loves the Kaffirs instead of loving his neighbor.

6.1.oldText: If now what has been developed here is correct, if there is nothing incommensurable in a human life, but the incommensurable that exists is so only by accident, from which nothing follows insofar as existence is regarded under the idea — then Hegel is right; but what he is not right about is to speak of faith, or to allow Abraham to be regarded as its father; for by the latter he has passed sentence both on Abraham and on faith. In Hegelian philosophy *das Äussere* (*die Entäusserung*) is higher than *das Innere*. This is often illustrated by an example. The child is *das Innere*; the man is *das Äussere*; hence the child is precisely determined by the outer, and conversely the man as *das Äussere* is precisely determined by *das Innere*. Faith, however, is this paradox: that inwardness is higher than outwardness, or — to recall once more an expression in the foregoing — that the odd number is higher than the even.

6.2.oldText: For the ethical view of life it is then the task of the single individual to strip himself of the determination of inwardness and to express this in an outward. Every time the single individual flinches from this, every time he wants to hold back in or slip back down into the determination of inwardness — feeling, mood, and so on — he commits an offense, then he lies in a temptation. The paradox of faith is this: that there is an inwardness which is incommensurable with the outward, an inwardness which, mark well, is not identical with the first one, but is a new

6.3.oldText: inwardness. This must not be overlooked. The newer philosophy has allowed itself, without further ado, to substitute the immediate for ‘faith.' When one does this, then it is ridiculous to deny that faith has existed at all times. Faith comes in this way into rather plain company with feeling, mood, idiosyncrasy, *vapeurs*, and so on. To this extent philosophy may be right that one ought not to stop there. But there is nothing that justifies philosophy in this use of language. Faith is preceded by a movement of infinity; only then does faith enter, *nec opinate*, by virtue of the absurd. This I can well understand, without, on that account, claiming that I have faith. If faith is nothing else than what philosophy makes it out to be, then Socrates already went further, far further, instead of the reverse — that he did not get to it. He has, in an intellectual respect, made the movement of infinity. His ignorance is the infinite resignation. This task is already a fitting one for human powers, even though our age scorns it; but only when it is done, only when the single individual has emptied himself in the infinite, only then has the point come where faith can break forth.

6.4.oldText: The paradox of faith, then, is this: that the single individual is higher than the universal — that the single individual, to recall a now rarer dogmatic distinction, determines his relation to the universal by his relation to the absolute, not his relation to the absolute by his relation to the universal. The paradox can also be expressed thus: that there is an absolute duty toward God; for in this duty-relation the single individual as the single individual relates himself absolutely to the absolute. So when in this connection it is said that it is a duty to love God, then something other is said than in the foregoing; for if this duty is absolute, then the ethical is reduced to the relative. From this, however, it does not follow that the ethical shall be annihilated; rather, it gets a quite different expression, the paradoxical expression, so that, for example, love of God can bring the knight of faith to give his love of the neighbor the opposite expression to what is, ethically speaking, duty.

6.5.oldText: If this is not so, then faith has no place in existence; then faith is a temptation, and Abraham is lost, since he gave in to it.

6.6.oldText: This paradox cannot be mediated; for it rests precisely on the fact that the single individual is only the single individual. As soon as this single individual wishes to express his absolute duty in the universal, becomes conscious of it in the universal, then he recognizes himself as being in a temptation, and then, if he otherwise puts up the resistance, he does not get to fulfill the so-called absolute duty; and if he does not, then he sins, even though his deed *realiter* turns out to be what was his absolute duty. What, then, was Abraham to do? If he had said to another person: Isaac I love higher than everything in the world, and that is why it is so heavy for me to sacrifice him — then the other would surely have shaken his head and said: why then will you sacrifice him? Or if the other had been a clever head, he would surely even have seen through Abraham, that he was putting on display feelings that stood in a heaven-shaking contradiction with his deed.

6.7.oldText: In the story of Abraham we find such a paradox. His relation to Isaac is, ethically expressed, this: that the father shall love the son. This ethical relation is reduced to the relative in opposition to the absolute relation to God. To the question why, Abraham has no other answer than that it is a trial, a temptation — which, as remarked above, is the unity of being for God's sake and for his own sake. These two determinations also correspond to each other in linguistic usage. So when one sees a person doing something that does not fit into the universal, one says: he hardly did that for God's sake; signifying thereby that he did it for his own sake. The paradox of faith has lost the middle term, i.e., the universal. On the one side it has the expression of the highest egoism (doing the dreadful thing he does for his own sake); on the other side, the expression of the most absolute devotion: doing it for God's sake. Faith itself cannot be mediated into the universal; for in that way it is annulled. Faith is this paradox, and the single individual cannot at all make himself understandable to anyone. People imagine that the single individual can make himself understandable to another single individual who is in the same case. Such a view would be unthinkable, were it not that in our age in so many ways one tries to sneak slyly into greatness. The one knight of faith cannot at all help the other. Either the single individual himself becomes a knight of faith by taking the paradox upon himself, or he never becomes one. Companionship in these regions is altogether unthinkable. Any closer explication of what is to be understood by Isaac the single individual can constantly give only to himself. And even if one could, ever so precisely, define generally what was to be understood by Isaac (which would moreover be the most ridiculous self-contradiction — to bring the single individual, who precisely stands outside the universal, under universal definitions, when he is to act precisely as the single individual who is outside the universal) — still the single individual could never assure himself of it through others, only through himself as the single individual. Therefore, even if a person were cowardly and wretched enough to want to become a knight of faith on someone else's word and surety, he still does not become one; for only the single individual becomes it as the single individual, and this is the great thing, which I can well understand without entering into it, since I lack the courage; but this is also the dreadful thing, which I can still better

6.8.oldText: There is presented, as is well known, in Luke 14:26, a remarkable doctrine concerning the absolute duty toward God: ‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and his mother, and his wife and his children, and his brothers and his sisters, yes, even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple.' This is a hard saying — who can bear to hear it? It is therefore also very rarely heard. Yet this silence is only a dodge, which helps not at all. The student of theology, however, comes to learn that these words occur in the New Testament, and in some exegetical aid he finds the information that *misein* in this and a couple of other passages stands per *meiosin* for: *minus diligo, posthabeo, non colo, nihili facio*. The connection in which these words occur, however, does not seem to support this tasteful explanation. For in the very next verse there is a story of how someone who would build a tower first makes an estimate to see whether he is able to do so, lest people afterward laugh at him. The close connection of this story with the verse just cited seems precisely to indicate that the words are to be taken as dreadfully as possible, so that everyone may test himself whether he can erect the building.

6.9.oldText: If that pious and soft-hearted exegete, who by haggling in this way thinks to smuggle Christianity into the world, were so fortunate as to convince a person that this was, both grammatically, linguistically, and *kat' analogian*, the meaning of that passage, then he will, hopefully, also have the good fortune in the same instant to convince that same person that Christianity is one of the most pitiable things in the world. For the doctrine that, in one of its most lyrical outbursts, where the consciousness of its eternal validity surges most strongly within it, has nothing else to say than a noisy word that means nothing, but only signifies that one shall be less benevolent, less attentive, more indifferent — the doctrine that, the moment it makes a face as if to say the dreadful, ends up cooling instead of terrifying — that doctrine is surely not worth standing up for.

6.10.oldText: The words are dreadful; yet I think that one can well understand them, without it following from this that the one who has understood them therefore has the courage to do it. One should be honest enough at least to acknowledge what stands there, to admit that it is the great thing, even if one does not oneself have the courage for it. He who behaves in this way shall not be excluded from sharing in the beautiful story; for it does, after all, contain in a way consolation for him who did not have the courage to begin building the tower. But he must be honest, and not explain this lack of courage as humility, since on the contrary it is pride — while the courage of faith is the only humble courage.

6.11.oldText: One easily sees now that if there is to be any meaning in the passage, it must be understood quite literally. God is the one who demands absolute love. The one who, in demanding a person's love, would mean that this love must also prove itself by his becoming lukewarm toward everything that was otherwise dear to him — he is not only an egoist, he is also stupid; and the one who would demand such a love thereby signs his own death warrant, insofar as he had his life in the love so coveted. A man demands, for example, that his wife shall leave father and mother; but if he were to consider it a proof of her extraordinary love for him that for his sake she became a lukewarm, sluggish daughter, and so on — then he is more stupid than the most stupid. If he had any conception of what love is, he would wish to discover and

6.12.oldText: see in it a security that his wife would love him as no one else in the kingdom, if he discovered that as a daughter and sister she was perfect in love.

6.13.oldText: What one would, then, in a person regard as a sign

6.14.oldText: of egoism and stupidity, that one is, with the help of an exegete, supposed to regard as a worthy conception of the deity.

6.15.oldText: But how, then, is one to hate them? I shall not here recall the human distinction either to love or to hate, not because I have so much against it, for it is at any rate passionate, but because it is egoistic and does not fit here. If, on the other hand, I regard the task as a paradox, then I understand it — i.e., I understand it the way one can understand a paradox. The absolute duty can then bring one to do what the ethical would forbid; but it can by no means bring the knight of faith to leave off loving. This Abraham shows. The moment he is to sacrifice Isaac, then the ethical expression for what he is doing is this: he hates Isaac. But if he really hated Isaac, he can be at peace that God does not demand this of him; for Cain and Abraham are not identical. Isaac he must love with all his soul; when God demands him, he must love him, if possible, even higher; and only then can he sacrifice him. For it is precisely this love for Isaac that, by its paradoxical opposition to his love for God, makes his deed a sacrifice. But this is the need and the anxiety in the paradox — that he, humanly speaking, cannot at all make himself understandable. Only at the moment when his deed is in absolute contradiction with his feeling — only then does he sacrifice Isaac; but the actuality of his deed is what makes him belong to the universal, and there he is and remains a murderer.

6.16.oldText: The passage in Luke must furthermore be understood in such a way that one perceives that the knight of faith does not get any higher expression whatever of the universal (as the ethical) in which he can save himself. So when one allowed the church to demand this sacrifice from one of its members, then we have only a tragic hero. For the idea of the church is not qualitatively different from that of the state, as soon as the single individual can enter it by a simple mediation; and as soon as the single

6.17.oldText: individual has entered into the paradox, he does not come to the idea of the church; he does not come out of the paradox, but must either find his blessedness in it, or his perdition. Such an ecclesiastical hero expresses in his deed the universal, and there shall be no one in the church, not even his father and mother and so on, who does not understand him. The knight of faith, however, he is not, and also has another answer than Abraham's; he does not say that it is a trial or a temptation in which he is being tested.

6.18.oldText: People generally refrain from citing such passages as the one in Luke. They fear letting people loose; they fear that the worst will happen, when first the single individual takes a fancy to *gerere* himself as the single individual. Furthermore, people think that to exist as the single individual is the easiest of all, and therefore one must precisely force people to become the universal. I can share neither that fear nor this opinion, and that for the same reason. The one who has learned that to exist as the single individual is the most dreadful of all shall not be afraid to say that it is the greatest, but he must also say it in such a way that his words scarcely become a snare for someone going astray, but rather help him into the universal, even if his words make a little room for the great. The one who dares not name such passages dares not name Abraham either; and to think that to exist as the single individual is easy enough contains a very dubious indirect concession with respect to oneself. For he who really has respect for himself and concern for his soul is convinced that the one who lives under his own supervision, alone in the whole world, lives more strictly and recluse than a girl in her bower. That there can be those who need compulsion, those who, if they were set at liberty, would like ungovernable beasts romp in selfish lust — that is true; but one shall precisely show that one does not belong to them by the fact that one knows how to speak with anxiety and trembling, and one shall speak out of reverence for the great, that it not be forgotten out of fear of the harm — which surely will not come, when one speaks in such a way that one knows it is the great, knows its terrors; and without this one does not know its greatness either.

6.19.oldText: Let us now consider a little more closely the need and the anxiety in the paradox of faith. The tragic hero resigns himself in order to express the universal; the knight of faith resigns the universal in order to become the single individual. As I said, everything depends on how one is situated. The one who thinks it is easy enough to be the single individual can always be sure that he is no knight of faith; for free birds and tramping geniuses are not men of faith. The knight of faith, on the other hand, knows that it is glorious to belong to the universal. He knows that it is beautiful and beneficial to be the single individual who translates himself into the universal — the one who, so to speak, himself produces a clean and elegant and as far as possible faultless edition of himself, legible for all. He knows that it is refreshing to become understandable to oneself in the universal, in such a way that he understands it, and every single individual who understands him in turn understands the universal in him, and both rejoice in the security of the universal. He knows it is beautiful to be born as the single individual who has his home in the universal, his friendly abiding place, which immediately receives him with open arms when he wants to remain in it. But he also knows that, higher than this, there twists a lonely path, narrow and steep; he knows it is dreadful to be born solitary out of the universal, to walk without meeting a single fellow traveler. He knows very well where he is, and how he stands related to people. Humanly speaking, he is insane and cannot make himself understandable to anyone. And yet to be insane is the mildest expression. If he is not regarded so, then he is a hypocrite, and the higher he climbs along the way, the more dreadful a hypocrite.

6.20.oldText: The knight of faith knows that it is inspiring to give up oneself for the universal, that it requires courage, but that there is also a security in it, precisely because it is for the universal; he knows that it is glorious to be understood by every noble person, and so understood that the spectator himself is ennobled by it. This he knows, and he feels himself bound, as it were; he could wish that this were the task that had been set for him. So Abraham could have wished, now and then, that the task were to love Isaac as befits a father, intelligible to all, unforgettable through the ages; he could wish that the task were to sacrifice Isaac for the universal, that he might inspire fathers to glorious deeds — and he is almost terrified at the thought that for him such wishes are only temptations and must be treated as such; for he knows it is a lonely way he treads, and that he accomplishes nothing for the universal, but is only being tested and tried himself. Or what did Abraham accomplish for the universal? Let me speak humanly about it, quite humanly! He uses seventy years to get a son in his old age. What others get quickly enough and have joy in for a long time, he uses seventy years to get; and why? because he is being tested and tempted. Is this not insanity! But Abraham believed, and only Sarah wavered and got him to take Hagar as a concubine; but for that reason he also had to drive her away. He gets Isaac — then he is to be tested again. He knew that it is glorious to express the universal, glorious to live with Isaac. But that is not the task. He knew that it is kingly to sacrifice such a son for the universal; he himself should have found rest in it, and all should have rested gloriously in his deed, as the vowel rests in its silent letter; but that is not the task — he is being tested. That Roman commander who is famous for his cognomen

6.21.oldText: Cunctator stopped the enemy by his hesitation — but what a delayer is Abraham in comparison with him — and yet he does not save the state. This is the content of one hundred and thirty years. Who can bear it? Should not his contemporaries — if there could be any question of such — say: ‘It is an eternal procrastination with Abraham; finally he got a son, that took long enough; now he wants to sacrifice him — is he not deranged? And if he could at least explain why he wants to do it, but always it is a trial.' Abraham could not explain more either; for his life is like a book under divine seal, which does not become *publici juris*.

6.22.oldText: This is the dreadful thing. He who does not see this can always be sure that he is not a knight of faith; but he who sees it shall not deny that even the most tested tragic hero walks as in a dance compared with the knight of faith, who only comes forward slowly and creeping. And when he has perceived this and assured himself that he does not have the courage to understand it, then he will perhaps sense the wondrous glory which that knight attains: that he becomes God's intimate, the Lord's friend — to speak quite humanly — that he says *Du* to God in heaven, while even the tragic hero only addresses Him in the third person.

6.23.oldText: The tragic hero is soon finished and has soon fought his fight; he makes the infinite movement and is now secured in the universal. The knight of faith, on the other hand, is kept sleepless; for he is constantly being tested, and at every moment there is a possibility of being able to return repentant to the universal, and this possibility may just as well be a temptation as truth. Information about this he can get from no human being; for then he is outside the paradox.

6.24.oldText: The knight of faith has, then, first and foremost, the passion to concentrate the entire ethical that he is breaking with into a single moment, that he may be able to give himself the assurance that he really loves Isaac with his whole soul *. If he cannot do this, then he lies in a temptation. Next, he has the passion to bring this entire assurance forth in an instant, and so that it is just as fully valid as in the first moment. If he cannot do this, then he gets nowhere from the spot, for then he must constantly begin again from the beginning. The tragic hero also concentrates the ethical that he teleologically has gone beyond into a single moment; but he has in this respect a foothold in the universal. The knight of faith has only and alone himself, and therein lies the dreadful. Most people live in an ethical obligation in such a way that they let each day have its own troubles; but they then never come to that passionate concentration, that energetic consciousness either. To get this, the universal can in a certain sense be of help to the tragic hero; but the knight of faith is alone with

6.25.oldText: everything. The tragic hero does it and finds rest in the universal; the knight of faith is constantly held in tension. Agamemnon gives up Iphigenia and has thereby found rest in the universal; he now proceeds to sacrifice her. If Agamemnon had not made the movement, if his soul in the decisive moment, instead of passionate concentration, had been lost in ordinary chatter — that he had several daughters, and that *vielleicht* yet *das Ausserordentliche* might happen — then he is not a hero, of course, but a mental patient. The hero's concentration Abraham also has, even though in him it is far harder, since he has no foothold in the universal at all; but he makes one more movement, by which he gathers his soul back upon the wonder. If Abraham has not done that, then he is only an Agamemnon — insofar, that is, as one can otherwise explain how it is to be defended that one would sacrifice Isaac when one thereby does no good for the universal.

6.26.oldText: Whether the single individual really lies in a temptation or whether he is a knight of faith — this only the single individual himself can decide. Yet one could construct out of the paradox some marks which can also be understood by the one who is not in it. The true knight of faith is always the absolute isolation; the inauthentic one is sectarian. This latter is an attempt to leap off from the narrow way of the paradox and become a tragic hero on the cheap. The tragic hero expresses the universal and sacrifices himself for it. Instead of doing this, the sectarian Master Jakel has a private theater, a few good friends and comrades who roughly represent the universal about as well as the staff-bearers in *The Golden Snuffbox* represent justice. The knight of faith, on the other hand, is the paradox; he is the single individual, absolutely the single individual without any connections or wide-ranging affiliations. This is the dreadful thing, which the sectarian wretch cannot endure. For instead of learning from this that he is not capable of doing the great, and then frankly admitting it — something I, of course, can only approve, since it is what I myself do — the bungler thinks that by joining together with a few other bunglers he will be able to do it. But it does not at all work; in the world of spirit no swindling is tolerated. A dozen sectarians take each other under the arm; they know nothing at all of the lonely temptations awaiting the knight of faith, and which he dare not flee, precisely because it would be still more dreadful if he presumptuously pressed forward. The sectarians drown each other out with noise and din; they keep anxiety away with their shouting; and such a hooting Deer-park company thinks it is storming heaven, and thinks it is going by the same way as the knight of faith, who in the loneliness of the universe never hears any human voice, but walks alone with his dreadful responsibility.

6.27.oldText: The knight of faith is referred to himself alone; he feels the pain of being unable to make himself understandable to others, but he feels no vain desire to want to instruct others. The pain is for him the assurance; the vain desire he does not know — for that he is too serious of soul. The inauthentic knight gives himself away easily by this mastery he has acquired in a moment. He does not at all grasp what it is about: that, insofar as another single individual is to walk the same way, he must in exactly the same way become the single individual, and then needs no one's instruction, least of all from one who would force himself upon him. Here, again, one leaps off; one cannot endure the martyrdom of unintelligibility, and instead of this one chooses, conveniently enough, the worldly admiration of mastery. The true knight of faith is a witness, never a teacher, and herein lies the deep humanity, which is worth more than this prattling sympathy for other people's woes and weals, which is honored under the name of sympathy, while it is nothing other than vanity. The one who only wants to be a witness thereby confesses that no person, not even the lowliest, needs another person's sympathy, or shall be debased thereby in order that another may be elevated. But just as he himself did not win what he won on the cheap, so he also does not sell it off cheaply; he is not wretched enough to take the admiration of people and in return give them his silent contempt — he knows that what is truly great is equally accessible to all.

6.28.oldText: Either, then, there is an absolute duty toward God; and if there is, it is the paradox described, that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal, and as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute — or else there has never been faith, because it has always existed; or else Abraham is lost; or else the passage in Luke 14 must be explained as that tasteful exegete explained it, and the corresponding passages, and the like, must be explained in the same way.

7.0.oldText: The ethical as such is the universal; as the universal it is, in turn, the manifest. The single individual, determined as immediate sensuous and psychic being, is the hidden. His ethical task is therefore to unwrap himself out of his hiddenness and become manifest in the universal. Every time he wishes, then, to remain in the hidden, he commits an offense and lies in temptation, out of which he comes only by revealing himself.

7.1.oldText: Here we stand again at the same point. If there is not a hiddenness which has its ground in the fact that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal, then Abraham's behavior cannot be defended; for he overlooked the ethical intermediary instances. If, on the other hand, there is such a hiddenness, then we stand at the paradox, which cannot be mediated, since it rests precisely on this — that the single individual as the single individual is higher than the universal, while the universal is precisely mediation. Hegelian philosophy admits no justified hiddenness, no justified incommensurability. It is, then, consistent with itself when it demands disclosure; but it is not clear with itself when it would regard Abraham as the father of faith and speak of faith. For faith is not the first immediacy, but a later one. The first immediacy is the aesthetic, and here Hegelian philosophy may well be right. But faith is not the aesthetic, or else faith has never existed, because it has always existed.

7.2.oldText: It will be best here to consider the whole matter purely aesthetically, and to that end to enter upon an aesthetic deliberation, in which I will ask the reader for the moment to give himself up entirely; while I, in order to contribute my share, will modify my presentation in relation to its objects. The category I will examine a little more closely is *the interesting* — a category which especially in our age, precisely because the age lives *in discrimine rerum*, has acquired great significance; for it is properly the category of the turning point. One should not therefore, as sometimes happens, after having oneself *pro virili* loved it, look down upon it because one has outgrown it; but neither ought one be too greedy for it; for it is certain that to become interesting, or that one's life is interesting, is not a task for industry, but a fateful privilege which, like every privilege in the world of spirit, is purchased only at the cost of deep pain. Thus Socrates was the most interesting man who has lived, his life the most interesting that has been led; but this existence was assigned to him by the deity, and insofar as he himself had to acquire it, he too was no stranger to toil and pain. To want to take such an existence in vain does not become anyone who thinks more seriously about life; and yet it is not rare in our age to see examples of such striving. The interesting is, by the way, a frontier category, a *confinium* between aesthetics and ethics. To this extent the deliberation must constantly graze the territory of ethics, while in order to acquire significance it must, with aesthetic inwardness and concupiscence, grasp the problem. Such a thing ethics in our age more rarely lets itself in for. The reason, it is said, is that there can be no place for it in the System. Then one could surely do it in monographs; and besides, if one will not do it at length, one can do it briefly, and yet attain the same thing — that is, if one has the predicate at one's command; for one or two predicates can betray a whole world. Should there in the System not be room for such little words?

7.3.oldText: Aristotle says in his immortal *Poetics*: *δύο μὲν οὖν τοῦ μύθου μέρη, περὶ ταῦτ᾽ ἐστι, περιπέτεια καὶ ἀναγνώρισις* (cf. ch. 11). It is naturally only the second moment that here occupies me: *anagnorisis*, recognition. Wherever there can be any question of recognition, there is *eo ipso* a question of a previous hiddenness. Just as recognition becomes the resolving, the relaxing element, so hiddenness is the suspenseful element in dramatic life. What Aristotle in the foregoing of the same chapter develops concerning the various values of the tragedy, all in relation to how *peripeteia* and *anagnorisis* glance off each other, and concerning the single and the double recognition — I cannot here take account of, even though it tempts by its inwardness and its quiet absorption, especially the one who has long enough been wearied by the superficial omniscience of the surveyors. A more general remark must here find its place. In Greek tragedy, hiddenness (and as a consequence of it, recognition) is an epic remnant which has its ground in a *fatum*, in which the dramatic action vanishes, and from which the action has its dim, riddling origin. From this comes the fact that the effect a Greek tragedy produces has a similarity with the impression of a marble statue that lacks the power of the eye. Greek tragedy is blind. Therefore a certain abstraction is required if one is rightly to be affected by it. A son murders his father, but only afterward does he learn that it was his father. A sister wants to sacrifice her brother, but in the decisive moment she learns of it. This kind of tragic can less occupy our reflective age. The newer drama has given up fate, has emancipated itself dramatically, is sighted, looks into itself, takes fate up into its dramatic consciousness. Hiddenness and disclosure are then the hero's free deed, for which he is responsible.

7.4.oldText: Also in the newer drama, recognition and hiddenness belong as an essential element. To cite examples of this would be too lengthy. I am polite enough to assume that everyone in our age who is so aesthetically lustful, so potent and inflamed, that he conceives just as easily as the partridge of which Aristotle speaks, who only needs to hear the cock's voice or its flight overhead — I assume that everyone, simply on hearing the word ‘hiddenness,' would easily shake half a dozen novels and comedies out of his sleeve. I can therefore be brief, and so will simply hint at a more general remark. If the one who plays at hiding, and thereby brings on the dramatic ferment of the piece, hides some nonsense, then we have a comedy; if, on the other hand, he stands in relation to the idea, then he can come close to becoming a tragic hero. Here just one example of the comic. A man wears makeup and a wig. The same man wishes to be a hit with the fair sex; he is sure enough of victory by the help of the makeup and the wig, which absolutely make him irresistible. He catches a girl and is at the height of happiness. Now comes the rub: can he confess it? Does he not lose all his bewitching power when he shows himself as a plain — yes, even a bald — man? Does he not thereby lose the beloved? — The hiddenness is his free action, for which aesthetics also makes him responsible. This science is no friend of bald

7.5.oldText: hypocrites; it surrenders him to laughter. This must be enough simply to indicate what I mean; the comic cannot be the subject of this investigation's interest.

7.6.oldText: The way I have to go is to carry hiddenness through dialectically by means of aesthetics and ethics; for it is essential that aesthetic hiddenness and the paradox show themselves in their absolute difference.

7.7.oldText: A pair of examples. A girl is secretly in love with someone, although they have not definitively confessed their love to one another. Her parents force her to marry another (there may also be a consideration of filial piety that determines her); she obeys her parents, she hides her love, ‘in order not to make the other unhappy, and no one shall ever come to know what she suffers.' — A young swain can, by a single word, come into possession of the object of his longings and his restless dreams. This little word, however, will compromise — yes, perhaps (who knows?) destroy — a whole family; he resolves magnanimously to remain in his hiddenness, ‘the girl shall never come to know it, that she may perhaps be happy by another's hand.' A pity that these two people, both of them each hidden from their respective beloveds, are also hidden from each other; otherwise a remarkable higher unity could here have been brought about. — Their hiddenness is a free deed, for which they are also responsible to aesthetics. Aesthetics, however, is a polite and sentimental science which knows more outlets than any pawnshop manager. What does it do, then? It does everything possible for the lovers. By the help of an accident, the respective partners in the projected marriage get a hint of the other party's magnanimous resolve; it comes to an explanation; they get each other, and along with it the rank of real heroes — for although they have not even had time to sleep on their heroic resolve, aesthetics regards them as if for many years they had courageously fought their resolve through. Aesthetics, you see, does not concern itself much about time, whether in jest or in earnest; time goes equally fast for it.

7.8.oldText: But ethics knows nothing either of that accident or of that sentimentality, nor has it so quick a concept of time. By this the matter takes on a different look. Ethics is not easy to dispute with, for it has clean categories. It does not appeal to experience, which is also of all ridiculous things just about the most ridiculous, and so far from making a man wise that it rather makes him crazy if he knows nothing higher than it. Ethics has no accident; therefore it does not come to an explanation; it does not jest with dignities; it lays an enormous responsibility on the slender shoulders of the heroes; it condemns as presumptuous the wish to play providence by one's deed, but it also condemns the wish to do it by one's suffering. It bids one believe in actuality and have courage to fight with all the troubles of actuality, rather than with these bloodless sufferings which one has taken upon oneself on one's own responsibility. It warns against believing the cunning calculations of the understanding, which are more faithless than the oracles of antiquity.
