It warns against every untimely magnanimity: let actuality take it, then is the time to show courage; but then ethics itself offers all possible assistance. If, however, it was something deeper that stirred in these two, if there was earnestness to see the task, earnestness to begin — then something will surely come of them; but ethics cannot help them, it is offended; for they have a secret from it, a secret they have taken on their own responsibility.

7.9.oldText: Aesthetics, then, demanded hiddenness and rewarded it; ethics demanded disclosure and punished hiddenness.

7.10.oldText: At times, however, aesthetics itself demands disclosure. When the hero, ensnared in the aesthetic illusion, thinks by his silence to save another person, then aesthetics demands silence and rewards it. When, on the other hand, the hero by his deed intervenes disturbingly in the life of another person, then aesthetics demands disclosure. Here I stand at the tragic hero. I will for a moment consider Euripides' *Iphigenia in Aulis*. Agamemnon is to sacrifice Iphigenia. Aesthetics demands silence of Agamemnon, insofar as it would be unworthy of the hero to seek consolation in another person, just as he, out of consideration for the women, ought to hide it from them as long as possible. On the other hand, the hero, precisely in order to be a hero, must also be tested in the dreadful temptation that the tears of Clytemnestra and Iphigenia will prepare for him. What does aesthetics do? It has a way out; it has an old servant ready who reveals everything to Clytemnestra. Now everything is in order.

7.11.oldText: Ethics, however, has no accident and no old servant at hand. The aesthetic idea contradicts itself as soon as it is to be carried out in actuality. Ethics therefore demands disclosure. The tragic hero shows precisely his ethical courage by being himself, not ensnared in any aesthetic illusion, the one who proclaims to Iphigenia her fate. If he does this, then the tragic hero is the beloved son of ethics, in whom she is well pleased. If he is silent, it may be because he thereby believes he is making it easier for others; but it may also be because he is making it easier for himself by it. Yet this he knows himself to be free of. If he is silent, then he as the single individual takes upon himself a responsibility, insofar as he overlooks an argument that may come from outside. This he as a tragic hero cannot do; for ethics loves him for that very reason, that he constantly expresses the universal. His heroic deed demands courage, but to this courage belongs also that he does not withdraw from any argumentation. Now it is certain that tears are a dreadful *argumentum ad hominem*, and there has surely been the man who was moved by nothing yet was moved by tears. In the play, Iphigenia gets leave to weep; in actuality there should be granted to her, as to Jephthah's daughter, two months in which to weep, not in solitude, but at her father's feet, and to use all her art, ‘which is only tears,' and to wind herself like an olive branch about his knees (cf. v. 1224).

7.12.oldText: Aesthetics demanded disclosure but helped itself out with an accident; ethics demanded disclosure, and found in the tragic hero its satisfaction.

7.13.oldText: In spite of the strictness with which ethics demands disclosure, it cannot be denied that secrecy and silence really make a person great, precisely because they are determinations of inwardness. When Amor leaves Psyche, he says to her: you shall bear a child, who shall be a divine child, if you are silent, but a human one, if you betray the secret. The tragic hero, who is ethics' favorite, is the pure human being; him I can also understand, and all his enterprise too is in the open. If I go further, then I constantly run up against the paradox, the divine and the demonic; for silence is both. Silence is the demon's snare; and the more one is silent, the more dreadful the demon becomes; but silence is also the deity's communion with the single individual,

7.14.oldText: before I, however, pass over to the story of Abraham, I will call forth a couple of poetic individualities. By the power of dialectics I keep them on the peak, and as I swing the discipline of despair over them, I shall surely keep them from standing still,

7.15.oldText: that, if possible, in their anxiety they may discover one or another thing *. Aristotle relates in his *Politics* a story of a political disturbance in Delphi, which had its ground in a marriage affair. The bridegroom, to whom the augurs predict a misfortune that will have its origin in his marriage, suddenly changes his plan in the decisive moment, when he comes to fetch the bride — he will not hold the wedding. I need no more. In Delphi this

7.16.oldText: These movements and postures may still become the object of aesthetic treatment; whether, however, faith and the whole life of faith can become so, I leave here undecided. I will only — because it is always a joy to me to thank the one to whom I owe something — thank Lessing for the few hints about a Christian drama that are found in his *Hamburgische Dramaturgie*. He has, however, fixed his gaze on the purely divine side of this life (the consummated victory), and therefore he has despaired; perhaps he would have judged otherwise had he paid more attention to the purely human side. (*Theologia viatorum*.) What he says is unmistakably very brief, in part evasive; but since I am always very glad when I can have an opportunity to bring Lessing in, I bring him in straightaway. Lessing was not only one of the most comprehensive heads Germany has owned; he was not only in possession of a quite rare promptness in his knowledge — which makes one able to rely securely on him and his autopsy without fearing being deceived by loose citations that have no place anywhere, half-understood phrases drawn from unreliable handbooks, or being disoriented by some stupid trumpeting of novelties which the older writers had set forth far better — he had besides a most uncommon gift for explaining what he himself had understood. There he stopped; in our age, people go further, and explain more than they themselves have understood.

7.17.oldText: event scarcely went off without tears; if a poet wished to adopt it, he could surely count on sympathy. Is it not dreadful, that love, which often enough has been an exile in life, is now also robbed of heaven's assistance? Is the old saying that marriage is established in heaven not put to shame here? Otherwise it is all the troubles and difficulties of finitude that, like evil spirits, would separate the lovers, while love has heaven on its side, and therefore this holy alliance conquers all enemies. Here it is heaven itself that separates what heaven itself has, after all, joined together. Who would have suspected this? Least of all, surely, the young bride. Only a moment ago she sat in her room in all her beauty, and the lovely girls had conscientiously decked her out so that they could answer for it before all the world, so that they had not only joy of it but envy — yes, joy that it was impossible for them to be more envious, because it was impossible for her to be more beautiful. She sat alone in her room, and was transformed from beauty to beauty; for everything that womanly art could achieve was used to deck out the worthy worthily; but there was still something lacking which the young girls had not dreamed of: a veil finer, lighter, and yet more concealing than that in which the young girls had wrapped her — a bridal robe of which no young girl knew, or could be of help in. The historical catastrophe was, according to Aristotle, the following: in order to revenge themselves, the family slip a temple-vessel in among his household goods, and he is condemned as a temple-

7.18.oldText: robber. This, however, is a matter of indifference; for the question is not whether the family is clever or stupid in taking revenge — the family acquires only ideal significance insofar as it is drawn into the hero's dialectic. It is, moreover, fateful enough that he, in trying to escape the danger by not marrying, plunges into it, and that his life in a double way comes into contact with the divine — first by the augur's saying, then by being condemned as a temple-robber. \[The bride was not even able to help herself.\] It was an invisible, friendly power that delights in adorning a bride that wrapped her in it, without her knowing anything of it; for she only saw the bridegroom go past and go up to the temple. She saw the door close behind him, and she became still calmer and more blissful; for she knew that he now belonged to her more than ever. The temple's door opened; he stepped out; but she lowered her eye in maidenly fashion, and so she did not see that his face was confused; but he saw that heaven was indeed envious of the bride's loveliness and his happiness. The temple's door opened; the young girls saw the bridegroom step out; but they did not see that his face was confused, for they were busy fetching the bride. Then she stepped forth in all her maidenly humility and yet as a sovereign, surrounded by her train of young girls, who curtsied to her, as the young girl always curtsies to a bride. So she stood at the head of the lovely company, and waited — it was only a moment, for the temple was right there — and the bridegroom came — but he passed by her door.

7.19.oldText: But I break off here; I am no poet, and only proceed dialectically. The first thing to note is that it is in the decisive moment that the hero gets that revelation; he is then pure and without remorse, has not frivolously bound himself to the beloved. Next, he has a divine pronouncement for him, or rather against him; he is then not, like those slender lovers and beloveds, governed by self-cleverness. It follows further as a matter of course that this pronouncement makes him just as unhappy as the bride — yes, a little more so, since he is, after all, the occasion. For while it is true that the augurs predicted only a misfortune to him, the question is whether this misfortune is not of such a kind that, in striking him, it will also strike their married happiness. What is he now to do? 1) Shall he be silent and hold the wedding, and think: misfortune perhaps does not come at once; in any case I have asserted my love and not feared to make myself unhappy; but be silent I must, or else even the brief moment is forfeited. This seems plausible, but it is by no means so; for in that case he has wronged the girl. He has by his silence in a way made the girl guilty; for if she had known of it, she surely would never have given her consent to such a union. He will then in the time of need have not only the misfortune to bear, but also the responsibility that he was silent — her just anger that he was silent. 2) Shall he be silent and refrain from holding the wedding? In that case he must enter upon a mystification by which he annihilates himself in his relation to her. This perhaps aesthetics would approve. The catastrophe could then be shaped after the manner of the actual one, only that in the last moment it would come to an explanation, which would, however, be after the fact, since aesthetically considered it becomes a necessity to let him die — unless this science should see itself able to lift that ill-omened prophecy. In the meantime this conduct, however magnanimous it may be, contains a wrong against the girl and the actuality of her love. 3) Shall he speak? One must of course not forget that our hero is a little too poetic for renouncing his love to have for him any other meaning than a failed business speculation. If he speaks, then the whole thing becomes an unhappy love story in the same style as Axel and Valborg *. They become a pair whom heaven itself

7.25.oldText: But to what end now this sketch, since after all I do not get further than to the tragic hero? Because it was, after all, possible that it might cast a light upon the paradox. Everything depends, then, on what relation he stands in to the augur's pronouncement, which in one way or another becomes decisive for his life. Is this pronouncement *publici juris* or is it a *privatissimum*? The scene is in Greece; an augur's pronouncement is intelligible to all — I do not mean only that the single individual can lexically understand the content, but that the single individual can understand that an augur announces to the single individual the decision of heaven. The augur's pronouncement is then intelligible not only to the hero, but to all, and there results no private relation to the deity from it. He can do whatever he will; what is foreshadowed will happen, and he comes neither by doing nor by leaving undone into a closer relation to the deity, becomes neither the object of its grace nor of its wrath. The outcome every single individual will be able to understand just as well as the hero, and there is no secret writing which only the hero can read. Insofar as he then wishes to speak, he can do so excellently, for he can make himself understandable; insofar as he wishes to be silent, it is because, by virtue of being the single individual, he wants to be higher than the universal — wants to dazzle himself with all sorts of fantastic notions about how she will soon forget the matter, and so on.

7.26.oldText: If, on the other hand, heaven's will had not been proclaimed to him by an augur, if it had come to his knowledge altogether privately, if it had set itself in an entirely private relation to him — then we are at the paradox, if it otherwise exists (for my consideration is dilemmatic); for then he could not speak, however gladly he would. He did not then enjoy himself in the silence, but he suffered the pain; but this very pain was for him the assurance that he was justified. His silence had then its ground not in his wishing as the single individual to set himself in an absolute relation to the universal, but in his being as the single individual placed in an absolute relation to the absolute. He would also be able to find rest in this, as I can imagine, while his magnanimous silence would constantly be disturbed by the demands of the ethical. It would, in general, be desirable if aesthetics one day would try to begin where, for so many years, it has ended — namely, with the illusory magnanimity. As soon as it did this, it would work right into the hands of the religious; for this power is the only one that can save the aesthetic out of its struggle with the ethical. Queen Elizabeth sacrificed her love for Essex to the state by signing his death warrant. This was a heroic deed, even if there was a little personal offense involved — that he had not sent her the ring. As is well known, he had done so, but by the malice of a lady-in-waiting it had been held back. Elizabeth received, so it is told *ni fallor*, the news of this; thereupon she sat for ten days with one finger in her mouth, biting it without saying a single word, and then she died. This was a task for a poet who knew how to wrench her mouth open; otherwise it is at most usable for a ballet master, with whom the poet in our age often enough confuses himself.

7.27.oldText: Now I will let a sketch follow in the direction of the demonic. For this I can use the legend of Agnes and the Merman. The merman is a seducer who shoots up out of the abyss's hiding-place, and in wild lust seizes and breaks the innocent flower that, in all its grace, stood at the seashore and pensively bent its head at the murmuring of the sea. This has so far been the poets' view. Let us make a change. The merman was a seducer. He has called Agnes; by his ingratiating speech he has lured forth the hidden in her; she has found in the merman what she sought, what she gazed after down at the bottom of the sea. Agnes wants to follow him. The merman has placed her on his arm; Agnes flings her arms about his neck; she gives herself trustingly with her whole soul to the stronger one. He stands already at the shore; he leans out over the sea to plunge down with his prey — then Agnes looks at him once more, not fearfully, not doubting, not proud of her happiness, not intoxicated with lust, but absolutely believing, but absolutely humble as the lowly flower she thought herself to be; absolutely trustingly she entrusts her whole fate to him with this glance. — And see! The sea no longer roars, its wild voice falls silent, the passion of nature, which is the merman's strength, leaves him in the lurch; it becomes a dead calm — and still Agnes looks at him in that way. Then the merman collapses; he cannot withstand the power of innocence; his element becomes faithless to him; he cannot seduce Agnes. 7.30.oldText: We will now give the merman a human consciousness, and let his being a merman signify a human pre-existence, in whose consequence his life was entangled. There is nothing to prevent him from becoming a hero, for the step he now takes is reconciling. He is saved by Agnes; the seducer is crushed; he has bowed under the power of innocence; he can never again seduce. But in the same instant two powers contend over him: repentance, and Agnes and repentance. If repentance takes him alone, then he is hidden; if Agnes and repentance take him, then he is manifest.

7.31.oldText: Insofar now as repentance takes hold of the merman and he remains hidden, then he has indeed made Agnes unhappy; for Agnes loved him in all her innocence; she believed it was true that, in that moment when he appeared changed even to her, however well he hid it, he only wanted to show her the beautiful stillness of the sea. The merman, however, even in respect to passion, becomes still more unhappy; for he loved Agnes with a multiplicity of passions, and besides has a new guilt to bear. The demonic in repentance will now indeed explain to him that this is precisely his punishment, and the more it tortures him the better.

7.32.oldText: If he gives himself up to this demonic, then he perhaps makes one more attempt to save Agnes — in the way that, in a certain sense, one can save a person by means of evil. He knows that Agnes loves him. Could he wrest from Agnes this love, then she would, in a way, be saved. But how? To count on this, that an open-hearted confession should awaken her revulsion — for that the merman is too clever. He will then perhaps see fit to inflame all dark passions in her, scorn her, mock her, make her love into a laughing-stock, if possible egg on her pride. He will not spare himself any torment, for this is the deep contradiction in the demonic; and there dwells, in a certain sense, infinitely more good in a demonic person than in trivial people. The more selfish Agnes is, the more easily will she be deceived (for it is only very inexperienced people who think it easy to deceive innocence; existence is most profound, and it is the easiest thing for the wise to dupe the wise) — but the more dreadful will the merman's sufferings be. The more cunningly his deception is laid, the less will Agnes bashfully hide her suffering from him; she will use every means, which then will not be without effect — that is, not to shake him, but to torment him.

A happy marriage! that is easy enough. \[He will have\] courage to wrest from himself every self-deception that he could make Agnes happy by his art; he will have courage, humanly speaking, to crush Agnes. The merman stands on a dialectical peak. If he is saved out of the demonic in repentance, then there are two ways possible. He can hold himself back, remain in the hidden, but not rely on his shrewdness. He does not then come, as the single individual, into an absolute relation to the demonic, but finds rest in the counter-paradox that the deity will save Agnes. (So the Middle Ages, surely, would make the movement; for the merman is, evidently, according to its concept, due to enter the cloister.) Or he can be saved by Agnes. This must now not be understood as if by Agnes's love he should be saved from becoming a seducer in the future (this is an aesthetic attempt at rescue, which always passes by the main thing — namely, the continuity of the merman's life); for in this respect he is saved; he is saved insofar as he becomes manifest. He then marries Agnes. In the meantime he must take refuge in the paradox. For when the single individual has, by his guilt, come outside the universal, then he can return to it only by virtue of being, as the single individual, in an absolute relation to the absolute. Here I will now make a remark by which I say more than has been said at any point in the foregoing **. Sin is not the first immediacy; sin is a later immediacy. In sin the single individual is already, in the direction of the demonic paradox, higher than the universal, because it is a contradiction of the universal to want to demand itself of the one who lacks the *conditio sine qua non*. If philosophy, among other things, also gave thought to the fact that it might occur to a person to want to act according to its teachings, then one would get a strange comedy out of it. An ethic that ignores sin is a perfectly idle science; but if it makes sin valid, then it is *eo ipso* beyond itself. Philosophy teaches that the immediate shall be annulled. This is true enough; but what is not true is that sin is, without further ado, the immediate, just as little as faith is, without further ado, the immediate. — A happy marriage! it is easy enough. If, on the other hand, ethics is to give the speech at the wedding, then I think it will be another matter. Aesthetics throws the cloak of love over the merman, and then everything is forgotten. It is also careless enough to think that it goes with a marriage as at an auction, where everything is sold in the condition in which it is found at the moment of the hammer-blow. If it would only see what happens afterwards — but for that it has no time; it is at once in full swing clapping a new loving pair together. Aesthetics is the most faithless of all the sciences. The merman's movements I can therefore understand, while I cannot understand Abraham; for the merman comes precisely through the paradox to want to realize the universal. For if he remains hidden and gives himself up to all the torments of repentance, then he becomes a demon, and as such is annihilated. If he remains hidden, but does not think shrewdly that by being himself tormented in the bondage of repentance he can work Agnes loose, then he gets peace, but he is lost to this world. If he becomes manifest, lets himself be saved by Agnes, then he is the greatest human being I can imagine; for it is only aesthetics that frivolously thinks to praise the power of love by letting the lost one be loved by an innocent girl and thereby saved; it is only aesthetics that sees wrongly, and believes that the girl is the heroine, instead of that the merman is. The merman cannot, then, belong to Agnes without his having, after making the infinite movement of repentance, made one more movement — the movement by virtue of the absurd. By his own strength he can make the movement of repentance; but he uses absolutely all his strength on it, and therefore he cannot, by his own strength, come back and grasp actuality. When one has not passion enough to make either the one or the other movement, when one slouches through life, repents a bit and thinks: the rest will go by itself — then one has, once and for all, renounced living in the idea, and then one can very easily attain, and help others attain, the highest, i.e., dazzle oneself and others into the notion that in the world of spirit it goes as in a game of *gnav*, where everything goes any which way. One can then amuse oneself by considering how strange it is that, precisely in an age when everyone, after all, can do the highest, doubt about the immortality of the soul can be so widespread; for he who has really made even the movement of infinity scarcely doubts. The conclusions of passion are the only reliable ones, i.e., the only convincing ones. Fortunately existence is here more loving, more faithful, than what wise men maintain; for it excludes no person, not even the lowliest; it cheats no one, for in the world of spirit only the one who cheats himself is cheated. It is the opinion of all, and insofar as I dare allow myself to judge of this, it is also my opinion, that it is not the highest to enter a cloister; but this is by no means therefore my opinion that in our age, when no one enters a cloister, everyone is greater than the deep and serious souls who found rest in a cloister. And it is incomprehensible that it has not already happened that the age itself, by a *generatio aequivoca*, has spawned its hero, the demon, who relentlessly will perform the dreadful drama: to make the whole age laugh, and to make it forget that it laughs at itself. And yet what higher movement has the age devised since the time when people gave up entering the cloister? Is it not a wretched life-wisdom, cleverness, faintheartedness, that sits in the high seat, that cowardly tells people they have done the highest, and slyly keeps them from even attempting the lesser? He who has made the cloister-movement has only one movement left, the movement of the absurd. How many in our age understand what the absurd is? How many in our age live in such a way that they have given up everything, or have got everything? How many are even so honest that they know what they can and what they cannot? And is it not true, that insofar as one finds such people, one finds them most readily among the less educated and partly among women? Should it really be that, that the age needs? Should the theater perhaps need a new play in which it would be made ridiculous that someone died of love? Or would it not rather be saving for the age, if it happened among us, if the age became witness to such an event — that it might at last get the courage to believe in the power of spirit, the courage not, cowardly, to stifle the better in oneself, enviously to stifle it in others — by laughter? 7.40.oldText: If one wanted a sketch in a similar style, which would, however, because the passion of repentance was not set in motion, become more touching, then one could use for it a story that occurs in the Book of Tobit. The young Tobias wishes to marry Sarah, the daughter of Raguel and Edna. With this girl there is a sad business. She has been given to seven men, all of whom have perished in the bridal chamber. This is, with respect to my sketch, a blemish in the story; for the comic effect is almost unavoidable when the thought is awakened of a girl's seven fruitless attempts to be married, even though she was quite close to it — as close as a student who has been failed seven times for the *Attestats*. In the Book of Tobit the accent lies elsewhere, and therefore the high number is of importance, and in a certain sense even tragically contributing; for so much the greater is the young Tobias's magnanimity, partly insofar as he is his parents' only son (6:15), partly because the deterrent more pressingly impinges. This must, then, be put aside. Sarah is then a girl who has never loved, who still carries within herself a young girl's blessedness, her enormous priority bond on existence, her *Vollmachtbrief zum Glücke* — to love a man with her whole heart. And yet she is more unhappy than anyone, for she knows that the evil demon who loves her will kill the bridegroom on the wedding night. I have read of much sorrow, but I doubt whether anywhere there is to be found such a deep sorrow as that which lies in this girl's life. When a misfortune comes from outside, then there is consolation to be found. Even if existence did not bring a person what could have made him happy, it is still a consolation that he could have received it. But the unfathomable sorrow which no time can disperse, no time heal — to know that it was no help, even if existence did everything! A Greek author hides in his simple naïveté so infinitely much when he says: *πάντως γὰρ οὐδεὶς Ἔρωτα ἔφυγεν ἢ φεύξεται, μέχρι ἂν κάλλος ᾖ καὶ ὀφθαλμοὶ βλέπωσιν* (cf. Longus, *Pastoralia*). There has been many a girl who became unhappy in love; but she did become so; Sarah was so before she became so. It is heavy not to find the one to whom one can give oneself, but it is unspeakably heavy not to be able to give oneself. A young girl gives herself, and then it is said: now she is no longer free; but Sarah was never free, and yet she had never given herself. It is heavy if a girl gave herself and was deceived; but Sarah was deceived before she gave herself. What sorrow of the world lies in what follows, when Tobias finally wishes to marry her! What wedding ceremonies, what preparations! No girl has been deceived as Sarah was; for she was deceived of the most blessed thing of all, the absolute wealth which even the poorest girl owns; deceived of the secure, unbounded, unbridled, unrestrained abandonment of self-giving. For first there was to be smoke, when the heart of the fish and the liver were laid on the glowing embers. And how must the mother not take leave of the daughter, who, like herself deceived of everything, must, in continuity with this, deceive the mother of the most beautiful thing? One only need read the story. Edna prepared the chamber and led Sarah into it, and wept, and received her daughter's tears. And she said to her: my child, be of good cheer! May the Lord of heaven and earth give you joy for this your sorrow! Daughter, be of good cheer. And now the wedding moment — let one read it, if one can for tears: but when they were both shut up together, Tobias rose up from the bed and said:

7.42.oldText: If a poet read this story, if he would use it, I would bet a hundred to one that he would lay everything on the young Tobias. The heroism of being willing to risk his life in such an evident danger — about which the story reminds us once more, for Raguel says the morning after the wedding to Edna: send one of the maidservants and let her see whether he is alive; but if not, that I may bury him, and no one shall know it (cf. 8:13) — this heroism would become the task. I take the liberty of proposing another. It is bold and brave and chivalrous of Tobias to act so; but every man who has not the courage for it is a sissy who knows neither what love is, nor what it is to be a man, nor what is worth living for; he has not even grasped the little mystery, that it is better to give than to receive, and has no inkling of the great mystery: that it is far harder to receive than to give — that is to say, when one has had courage to do without, and in the time of need was not cowardly. No, Sarah is the heroine. Her I will draw near to, as I have never drawn near to any girl, nor felt myself tempted in thought to draw near to any I have read about. For what love of God is required, in order to want to let oneself be healed when one is in this way from the beginning unhinged through no fault of one's own — from the beginning a botched specimen of a human being! What ethical maturity to take upon oneself the responsibility of permitting the beloved such a daring venture! What humility before another person! What faith in God, that she should not in the next moment hate the man to whom she owed everything!

7.43.oldText: Let Sarah be a man, and the demonic lies right at hand. The proud, noble nature can endure everything; but one thing it cannot endure — it cannot endure

7.44.oldText: compassion. There lies a wrong in it, which can only be inflicted on him by a higher power; for by himself he can never become its object. If he has sinned, he can bear the punishment without despairing; but to be without guilt singled out from his mother's womb as the object of compassion, a sweet smell in its nostrils — this he cannot endure. Compassion has a strange dialectic; in one moment it demands guilt, in the next it will not have it; and therefore being predestined to compassion becomes more and more dreadful, the more the individual's misfortune is in the direction of the spiritual. But Sarah has no guilt; she is thrown out as prey to all sufferings, and on top of that she must be tortured by people's compassion; for even I, who admire her more than Tobias loved her, even I cannot mention her name without saying: poor girl. Let a man be in Sarah's place; let him know that, if he will love a girl, then a hellish spirit will come and murder the beloved on the wedding night — then it is well possible that he chose the demonic; he closed himself up in himself, and said in the way a demonic nature speaks in secret: ‘Thank you, I am no friend of ceremonies and elaborateness; I do not at all desire the joy of love; I might as well become a Bluebeard, who has his delight in seeing girls sink down on the wedding night.' One generally learns very little about the demonic, although this region precisely in our age has a valid claim to be discovered, although the observer, when he otherwise knows how to set himself in a little rapport with the demon, can almost use any person at least momentarily. Shakespeare is and always remains, in this direction, a hero. That dreadful demon, the most demonic figure Shakespeare has portrayed, but also portrayed matchlessly — Gloucester (afterward Richard the Third) — what made him a demon? Plainly this: that he could not bear compassion, to which from childhood he had been given over. His monologue in the first act of *Richard the Third* is worth more than entire moral systems, which have no inkling of the terrors of existence, or of the explanation.
