7.46.oldText: Such natures as Gloucester's one cannot save by mediating them into an idea of society. Ethics really only mocks them — as it would be a mockery of Sarah if it were to say to her: why do you not express the universal and get married? Such natures are from the bottom of their being in the paradox; and they are by no means more imperfect than other people, only that they are either lost in the demonic paradox or saved in the divine. People have, on and off, taken pleasure in the fact that witches, gnomes, trolls, and the like were misshapen creatures; and it cannot be denied that every person has a tendency, when he sees a misshapen person, at once to attach to it the conception of a moral depravity. What an enormous injustice — since the relationship must rather be inverted: existence itself has corrupted them, as a stepmother makes the children unruly. Originally, by nature or historical condition, to be set outside the universal — that is the beginning of the demonic, of which the individual is not himself guilty. Cumberland's *The Jew* is in this way also a demon, even if he does what is good. So the demonic can also express itself as contempt for people — a contempt which, mark well, does not bring the demonic person himself to act contemptibly; on the contrary, he has his strength in knowing that he is better than all who judge him. — Concerning all such things the poet ought first and foremost to raise an alarm. God knows what writings the now-living younger versifiers read! Their study probably consists in learning rhymes by heart. God knows what their significance in existence is! At this moment I do not know that they are of any other use than that they furnish an edifying proof of the soul's immortality, since one can confidently say of them to oneself what Baggesen says of the city's poet Kildevalle: if he becomes immortal, then we all become so. — What has been said here in connection with Sarah, mainly in the direction of poetic production, and therefore with a fantastic presupposition, has its full meaning when one would, with psychological interest, sink into the meaning of the old saying: *nullum unquam exstitit magnum ingenium sine aliqua dementia*. For this *dementia* is the genius's suffering in existence — is the expression for, if I dare put it so, the divine envy, while the genial is the expression of preferential love. Thus the genius is from the beginning disoriented in relation to the universal, and brought into relation to the paradox — whether, in despair over his limitation, which in his eyes transforms his omnipotence into impotence, he seeks a demonic appeasement and therefore will not acknowledge it either before God or before people, or whether he religiously calms himself in love for the deity. Here lie psychological tasks on which, it seems to me, one might gladly sacrifice an entire life; and yet so seldom does one hear a word about them. In what relation does mental derangement stand to genius? Can one construct the one out of the other? In what sense and to what extent is the genius master over his derangement? For it follows of itself that he, to a certain degree, is master over it, since otherwise he really would be deranged. To such observations, however, belong shrewdness in a high degree and love; for to observe the superior is most difficult. If with attention to this one would read through some of the most genial authors, then it might still be possible, just very seldom and even with much trouble, to discover a little.

7.47.oldText: One more case I will think of, that a single individual by being hidden and by his silence wishes to save the universal. For this I can use the legend of Faust. Faust is a doubter, a spirit's apostate, who walks the way of the flesh.

7.48.oldText: This is the poets' view; and although it is repeated again and again that every age has its Faust, still one of its poets after another walks unwearied along the well-trodden highway. Let us undertake a small alteration. Faust is the doubter *kat' exochen*; but he is a sympathetic nature. Even in Goethe's interpretation of Faust, I miss a deeper psychological insight into the secret conversations of doubt with itself. In our age, when after all everyone has experienced doubt, no poet has yet taken a step in this direction. I think therefore I might safely offer them royal stationery to write on, in order to write down all the much they in this respect have experienced — they would scarcely write more than would fit on the very front margin.

7.49.oldText: Only when one in this way bends Faust into himself, only then can doubt take itself out poetically, only then does he properly discover, in actuality, all its sufferings. He knows then that it is spirit that bears existence, but he also knows that the security and joy in which people live are not grounded in the power of spirit, but easily explainable as unreflected blissfulness. As doubter, as the doubter, he is higher than all this; and if anyone would deceive him by making him believe that he had passed through doubt, he easily sees through it; for he who has made a movement in the world of spirit — that is, an infinite movement — he can immediately

7.50.oldText: existence. I demand, then, this magnanimity of him; but if he has it, dare he then be silent? Ethics is a dangerous science; and it would well be possible that Aristophanes, determined purely ethically, has resolved to let laughter pass judgment on the deluded age. Aesthetic magnanimity cannot help, for on that score one does not venture such a thing. If he is to be silent, then he must enter into the paradox. — One more sketch I will indicate: that, for example, a person possesses an explanation of a hero's life, which in a sad way explains it, and yet a whole age rests absolutely securely in this hero, without suspecting any such thing.

7.51.oldText: hear through the line, whether it is a tested man speaking, or a Munchausen. What a Tamerlane can do with his Huns, that Faust knows he can do with his doubt — to startle people up in horror, to let existence sway under their feet, to splinter people apart, to make the cry of anxiety sound everywhere. And if he does it, then he is, after all, no Tamerlane; he is in a certain sense authorized, and has the authorization of thought. But Faust is a sympathetic nature; he loves existence; his soul knows no envy; he sees that he cannot stop the raging he can well awaken; he covets no Herostratic glory — he is silent; he hides the doubt in his soul more carefully than the girl who hides the fruit of a sinful love beneath her heart; he tries as well as he can to keep step with other people; but what goes on in him he consumes within himself, and so he brings himself as a sacrifice for the universal.

7.52.oldText: One can sometimes hear people lament when an eccentric head sets the whirl of doubt going; they then say: would that he had been silent! This idea Faust realizes. He who has any conception of what it means that a person lives by spirit also knows what the hunger of doubt means, and that the doubter hungers just as much for daily bread as for spiritual nourishment. Even though, then, all the pain Faust suffers can be a quite good argument that it is not pride that has possessed him, still I will use a small precaution which I easily devise; for as Gregory of Rimini was called *tortor infantium*, because he assumed the damnation of small children, so I might be tempted to call myself *tortor heroum*, for I am very inventive when it comes to torturing the heroes. Faust sees Margaret — not after he has chosen lust, for my Faust does not choose lust at all; he sees Margaret not in Mephistopheles' concave mirror, but in all her lovely innocence; and since his soul has preserved love for people, he can also very well fall in love with her. But he is a doubter; his doubt has annihilated actuality for him; for so ideal is my Faust that he does not belong to those scientific doubters who doubt for one hour each semester at the lectern, but otherwise can do everything else, just as they do this — without the condition of spirit, or by virtue of spirit. He is a doubter, and the doubter hungers just as much for joy's daily bread as for spirit's food. Yet he remains true to his resolve and is silent, and speaks to no person about his doubt, and to Margaret either of his love.

7.53.oldText: It follows of itself that Faust is too ideal a figure to put up with the chatter that, if he spoke, he would occasion a general discussion, or the whole thing would pass off without consequence, or perhaps, or perhaps. (Here slumbers, as every poet will easily see, the comic in the sketch — by bringing Faust into an ironic relation to those low-comic fools who in our age run after doubt, who put forth an outward argument that they really have doubted — for example, a doctor's certificate — or swear that they have doubted everything, or prove it by the fact that on their journey they fell in with a doubter; these expresses and quick-runners in the world of spirit, who in great haste pick up at one person a little inkling of doubt, at another of faith, and now *wirthschaften* in the best way, just as the parish wants fine sand or coarse.) Faust is too ideal a figure to walk in train. He who has not an infinite passion is not ideal, and he who has an infinite passion has long since saved his soul out of such drivel. He is silent in order to sacrifice himself — or he speaks with the consciousness that he will confuse everything.

7.54.oldText: If he is silent, then ethics passes judgment on him; for it says:

7.55.oldText: ‘You shall acknowledge the universal, and you acknowledge it precisely by speaking, and you dare not have compassion on the universal.' This consideration one ought not to forget when one occasionally judges a doubter strictly because he speaks. I am not inclined to judge such conduct mildly; but here, as everywhere, it depends on the movements being made normally. If wrong is to be done, then a doubter — even if by speaking he brought all possible misfortune upon the world — is far to be preferred to those wretched sweet-tooths who taste everything, and who would cure doubt without knowing it, and who therefore generally are the proximate occasion for doubt's breaking forth wildly and ungovernably. — If he speaks, then he confuses everything; for whether or not it happens, he learns only afterward, and the outcome cannot help one — neither in the moment of action, nor with respect to responsibility.

7.56.oldText: If he is silent on his own responsibility, then he can indeed act magnanimously; but to his other pain he will feel a small temptation; for the universal will constantly torment him and say: you should have spoken; where will you find the certainty that it was not, after all, a hidden pride that governed your decision?

7.57.oldText: If, on the other hand, the doubter can become the single individual who as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute, then he can get an authorization for his silence. In that case he must make his doubt into guilt. In that case he is in the paradox; but in that case his doubt is healed, even if he might get another doubt.

7.58.oldText: Even the New Testament would acknowledge such a silence. There even occur passages in the New Testament that praise irony, only that it is used to hide the better. This movement, however, is just as much that of irony as of anything else that has its ground in the fact that subjectivity is higher than actuality. This our age will know nothing of; it will, in general, know nothing more about irony than what Hegel has said, who, oddly enough, did not understand much about it, and bore a grudge against it, which our age has good reason not to give up; for it must merely beware of irony. It is said in the Sermon on the Mount: when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that people may not see that you are fasting. This passage testifies plainly that subjectivity is incommensurable with actuality, indeed that it has the right to deceive. If only those people who in our age go feeling around with loose talk about the idea of the congregation would read the New Testament, then they might perhaps come to other thoughts.

7.59.oldText: But now Abraham — how did he act? For I have not forgotten, and the reader will now perhaps be pleased to remember, that it was in order to come up against this that I let myself in for the whole foregoing investigation — not as if Abraham would by it become more intelligible, but in order that the unintelligibility might become more desultory; for, as I said, Abraham I cannot understand, him I can only admire. It was also remarked that none of the stages described contained an analogy to Abraham; they were only developed so that, while they were shown within their own sphere, they might in the moment of misalignment, as it were, indicate the boundary of the unknown land. Insofar as there should be any question of an analogy, it would have to be the paradox of sin; but this lies again in another sphere, and cannot explain Abraham, and is itself far more easily explained than Abraham.

7.60.oldText: Abraham, then, did not speak; he did not speak to Sarah, not to Eliezer, not to Isaac; he passed by the three ethical instances. For the ethical had for Abraham no higher expression than family life.

7.61.oldText: Aesthetics permitted — yes, demanded — silence of the single individual when by his silence he could save another.

7.62.oldText: This already shows sufficiently that Abraham does not lie within the compass of aesthetics. His silence is by no means in order to save Isaac; just as, in general, his whole task — to sacrifice Isaac for his own and for God's sake — is an offense to aesthetics; for aesthetics can well understand that I sacrifice myself, but not that I sacrifice another for my own sake. The aesthetic hero was silent. Ethics, however, judged him because he was silent by virtue of his accidental singularity. It was his human foreknowledge that determined him to be silent. This ethics cannot forgive; every such human knowledge is only an illusion; ethics demands an infinite movement; it demands disclosure. The aesthetic hero, then, can speak, but will not.

7.63.oldText: The real tragic hero sacrifices himself and all that is his for the universal; his deed, every emotion in him, belongs to the universal; he is manifest, and in this disclosure ethics' beloved son. This does not fit Abraham; he does nothing for the universal, and he is hidden.

7.64.oldText: Now, then, we stand at the paradox. Either the single individual as the single individual can stand in an absolute relation to the absolute, and then the ethical is not the highest; or else Abraham is lost: he is neither a tragic hero nor an aesthetic hero.

7.65.oldText: To this extent it can again seem here that the paradox is the easiest and most convenient of all. Meanwhile I must repeat that the one who holds himself convinced of this is not a knight of faith; for need and anxiety are the only justification that can be conceived, even if it cannot be conceived universally — for then the paradox is annulled.

7.66.oldText: Abraham is silent — but he cannot speak; therein lie the need and the anxiety. For when, as I am speaking, I cannot make myself understandable, then I am not speaking, even if I went on speaking uninterruptedly night and day. This is Abraham's case. He can say everything; but one thing he cannot say; and yet, when he cannot say it — i.e., say it in such a way that another understands it — then he is not speaking. The relieving thing about speech is that it translates me into the universal. Now Abraham can say the most beautiful things any language can produce about how he loves Isaac. But this is not what lies on his mind; it is the deeper thing — that he wants to sacrifice him because it is a trial. This last no one can understand, and so anyone can only misunderstand the first. This need the tragic hero does not know. He has, in the first place, the consolation that every counter-argument has had its due — that he has been able to give Clytemnestra, Iphigenia, Achilles, the chorus, every living being, every voice from the heart of mankind, every cunning, every anxious, every accusing, every compassionate thought the chance to rise up against him. He can be sure that everything that could be said against him has been said, mercilessly, pitilessly — and to fight against the whole world is a consolation; to fight with oneself is dreadful — he need not fear that he has overlooked anything; that one day afterwards he must perhaps cry out as did King Edward IV at the news of Clarence's murder:

7.67.oldText: *Wer bat für ihn? Wer kniet' in meinem Grimm / Zu Füssen mir und bat mich überlegen? / Wer sprach von Bruderpflicht? Wer sprach von Liebe?*

7.68.oldText: The tragic hero does not know the dreadful responsibility of solitude. Next, he has the consolation that he can weep and lament with Clytemnestra and Iphigenia — and tears and cries assuage, but unutterable sighs torture. Agamemnon can quickly gather his soul into the certainty that he will act, and then he still has time to console and to encourage. This Abraham cannot do. When his heart is moved, when his words would contain a blessed comfort for the whole world, he dare not console; for would not Sarah, would not Eliezer, would not Isaac say to him: ‘Why then would you do it? you can leave it undone.' And if then in his need he wanted to give vent to his feelings, wanted to embrace everything that was dear to him before he proceeded to the last, then he might bring about the dreadful thing that Sarah, that Eliezer, that Isaac were offended at him and thought him a hypocrite. Speak he cannot; he speaks no human language. Even if he himself understood all the tongues of earth, even if the beloved understood them too, he still cannot speak — he speaks in a divine tongue, he speaks in tongues.

7.69.oldText: This need I can well understand; I can admire Abraham; I do not fear that anyone, by reason of this story, will be tempted frivolously to want to be the single individual; but I confess too that I do not have the courage for it, and that I gladly renounce every prospect of going further, if only it were possible that I should ever, however late, get so far. At every moment Abraham can break off; he can repent the whole thing as a temptation; then he can speak; then everyone can understand him — but then he is no longer Abraham.

7.70.oldText: Abraham cannot speak; for he cannot say (i.e., so that it is intelligible) that which would explain everything: that it is a trial — and, mark well, such a one in which the ethical is the temptation. He who is so placed is an emigrant from the sphere of the universal. But the next thing he can still less say. For Abraham makes, as has earlier been sufficiently developed, two movements. He makes the infinite movement of resignation and gives up Isaac — this no one can understand, because it is a private undertaking. But next he makes at every moment faith's

7.71.oldText: movement. This is his consolation. For he says, i.e.:

7.72.oldText: yet it will not happen, or if it happens, then the Lord will give me a new Isaac — by virtue, that is, of the absurd. The tragic hero, after all, gets to the end of the story. Iphigenia bows under her father's resolve; she herself makes the infinite movement of resignation, and they are now in understanding with each other. She can understand Agamemnon, because his enterprise expresses the universal. If Agamemnon were, on the other hand, to say to her: ‘Even though the god demands you as a sacrifice, it is still possible that he does not demand it — by virtue, that is, of the absurd' — then he would in the same moment become unintelligible to Iphigenia. If he could say it by virtue of human calculation, then Iphigenia would surely understand him; but then it would follow that Agamemnon had not made the infinite movement of resignation, and then he is not a hero — then the seer's saying is a piece of skipper's gossip, and the whole event is a vaudeville.

7.73.oldText: Abraham, then, did not speak. Only one word of his is preserved — the only line he says to Isaac, which also sufficiently proves that he had not spoken before. Isaac asks Abraham where the lamb for the burnt offering is. ‘And Abraham said: God will see to the lamb for the burnt offering, my son!'

7.74.oldText: This last word of Abraham I will here consider a little more closely. Were this word not, then the whole event would be lacking something; were it otherwise, then everything would perhaps dissolve into confusion.

7.75.oldText: It has often been the object of my deliberation how far a tragic hero, whether he culminates in a suffering or in an action, ought to have a final word. It depends, as far as I can judge, on the sphere of life to which he belongs, on how far his life has intellectual significance, on how far his suffering or action stands in relation to spirit.

7.76.oldText: It follows of itself that the tragic hero in his

7.77.oldText: culminating moment, like every other person who has not been deprived of speech, can say a few words, perhaps a few fitting words; but the question is how far it is fitting for him to say them. If the meaning of his life lies in an outward deed, then he has nothing to say; then everything he says is essentially chatter, by which he only weakens the impression of himself, while the tragic ceremonial commands that he silently fulfill his task — whether this consists in a deed or a suffering. Not to go too far, I will only take what lies most immediately at hand. If Agamemnon himself, not Calchas, were to draw the knife against Iphigenia, then he would only have demeaned himself by, in the last moment, wanting to say a few words; for the meaning of his deed was, after all, evident to all; the procedure of piety, of pity, of feeling, of tears was completed; and besides, his life had no relation to spirit, i.e., he was no teacher or witness of spirit. If, on the other hand, the meaning of a hero's life is in the direction of spirit, then the lack of a line would weaken the impression of him. What he then has to say is not a few fitting words, a little declamation piece, but the meaning of his line is that he carries himself through in the decisive moment. Such an intellectual tragic hero ought to have, and ought to keep, the last word. One demands of him the same transfigured bearing that befits every tragic hero; but then one demands one more word. Insofar, then, as such an intellectual tragic hero culminates in a suffering (in death), then in this last word he becomes immortal before he dies — while, on the contrary, the ordinary tragic hero only becomes immortal after his death. One can use Socrates as an example. He was an intellectual tragic hero. His death sentence is announced to him. In that moment he dies; for he who does not understand that the whole power of the spirit is required to die, and that the hero always dies before he dies, will not get very far in his consideration of life. Now, as a hero, it is required of Socrates that he rest calmly in himself; but as an intellectual tragic hero, it is required of him that in this last moment he have spirit-strength enough to carry himself through. He cannot then, like the ordinary tragic hero, concentrate on holding himself up over against death, but he must so quickly make this movement that in the same moment with his consciousness he is past this struggle and asserts himself. Thus, if Socrates in death's crisis had become silent, he would have weakened the effect of his life, awakened a suspicion that the elasticity of irony in him was not a world-power, but a play whose resilience in the decisive moment would have to be used in inverse measure to hold him up pathetically *.

7.78.oldText: What has here been briefly hinted at cannot indeed find its application to Abraham, insofar as one means that by some analogy one might be able to find a fitting word for Abraham to end with; but rather insofar as one perceives the necessity that Abraham in the last moment must carry himself through, must not silently draw the knife, but must have a word to say, since as the father of faith he has absolute significance in the direction of spirit. What he is to say, of that I can form no conception in advance; after he has said it, then I can well understand, well in a certain sense understand Abraham in the

7.79.oldText: Which line of Socrates' is to be regarded as the decisive one — about that opinions can be divided, since Socrates has in so many ways been poetically transfigured by Plato. I propose the following: the death sentence is announced to him; in the same moment he dies; in the same moment he overcomes death and carries himself through in the famous reply: that it surprised him that he had been condemned by a majority of three votes. With no loose and idle talk in the marketplace, with no foolish remark of an idiot, could he have jested more ironically than with that death sentence which condemles him himself from life.

7.80.oldText: matter, without thereby being any closer to him than I have been to him in the foregoing. If there had existed no last line of Socrates, then I could have thought myself into him and formed such a one; if I could not have done it, a poet could have managed it; but Abraham no poet can reach.

7.81.oldText: Before I pass over to a closer consideration of Abraham's last words, I must first call attention to the difficulty of Abraham's being able to come to say anything at all. The need and the anxiety in the paradox lay, as developed above, precisely in the silence: Abraham cannot speak *. To this extent it is, then, a self-contradiction to demand that he should speak — unless one wishes to have him out again of the paradox, in such a way that he in the decisive moment suspends it, by which he then ceases to be Abraham and annuls the whole foregoing. Thus, if Abraham now in the decisive moment were to say to Isaac: it is you, the matter concerns — then this would only be a weakness. For if he could speak at all, then he would have had to speak long before, and the weakness would lie in his not having had spirit's maturity and concentration to think through the whole pain in advance, but had pushed something away from himself, so that the actual pain was a *more* than the thought one. Besides, he would by such a speech fall out of the paradox; and if he really wanted to speak with Isaac, he would have to transform his condition into a temptation; for otherwise he could after all say nothing; and if he does this, then he is not even any kind of tragic hero.

7.82.oldText: Meanwhile a final word of Abraham is, after all, preserved; and insofar as I can understand the paradox, I can

7.83.oldText: * Insofar as there can be any question of an analogy, Pythagoras's death-situation provides one; for the silence he had always maintained he had to carry through in his last moment, and therefore he said: it is better to be killed than to speak. Cf. Diogenes, Book 8, §39.

7.84.oldText: also understand Abraham's total presence in this word. He says, first and foremost, nothing; and in this form he says what he has to say. His answer to Isaac has the form of irony, for it is always irony when I say something and yet say nothing. Isaac asks Abraham, in the conviction that Abraham knows. If Abraham now were to have answered: I know nothing — then he would have said an untruth. Say something he cannot, for what he knows he cannot say. He answers, then: God will see to the lamb for the burnt offering, my son! One sees from this the double movement in Abraham's soul, as it has been described in the foregoing. Had Abraham only resigned Isaac and not done more, then he would have said an untruth; for he knows, after all, that God demands Isaac as a sacrifice, and he knows that he himself precisely in this moment is ready to sacrifice him. He has, then, at every moment, after having made this movement, made the next — has made the movement of faith by virtue of the absurd. To this extent he says no untruth; for by virtue of the absurd, it is, after all, possible that God could do something quite different. He says, then, no untruth; but neither does he say anything — for he speaks in a foreign tongue. This becomes still more evident when we consider that it was Abraham himself who was to sacrifice Isaac. Had the task been a different one — had the Lord commanded Abraham to bring Isaac out to Mount Moriah, where the Lord himself would let his lightning strike Isaac and so take him as a sacrifice — then Abraham could in the straightforward sense have been right to speak as enigmatically as he does; for then he himself could not have known what would happen. But as the task is set for Abraham, he is himself to act; he must therefore in the decisive moment know what he himself will do, and so he must know that Isaac is to be sacrificed. If he has not known this with definiteness, then he has not made the infinite movement of resignation; then his word is indeed not an untruth, but he is also very far from being Abraham — he is more insignificant than a tragic hero; indeed, he is an irresolute man, who can decide neither for the one nor for the other, and who on that account will always come to speak in riddles. But such a hesitator is precisely the parody of the knight of faith.

7.85.oldText: It shows itself again here that one can well understand Abraham, but understand him only in the way one understands the paradox. I, for my part, can well understand Abraham; but I also grasp that I do not have the courage to speak in this way, just as little as I have the courage to act as Abraham did; but by this I by no means say that it is something insignificant, since on the contrary it is the only wondrous thing.

7.86.oldText: And what did the contemporary age judge of the tragic hero? That he was great, and it admired him. And that venerable assembly of the noble, the jury which every generation constitutes to judge the previous generation — it judged the same. But Abraham there was no one who could understand. And yet what did he attain? That he remained true to his love. But he who loves God needs no tears, no admiration; he forgets the suffering in the love — yes, so completely has he forgotten it, that there should not even afterward be the slightest hint of his pain, if God himself did not remember it; for he sees in secret, and knows the need, and counts the tears, and forgets nothing.

7.87.oldText: Either, then, there is a paradox: that the single individual as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute; or else Abraham is lost.

8.0.oldText: Once, in Holland, when the prices of spices became somewhat sluggish, the merchants had a couple of cargoes sunk in the sea in order to screw up the price. This was a forgivable, perhaps a necessary deception. Is it something similar that we need in the world of spirit? Are we so convinced that we have come to the highest, that there is nothing else left but piously to make ourselves believe that we have not come so far, only in order to find something with which to fill out the time? Is it such a self-deception that the present generation needs? Is it for a virtuosity in this that it is to be educated? Or is it not, rather, sufficiently perfected in the art of deceiving itself? Or is what it needs not, rather, an honest seriousness which fearlessly and incorruptibly points to the tasks — an honest seriousness which lovingly safeguards the tasks, which does not frighten people into trying to startle themselves into the highest, but keeps the tasks young and beautiful and lovely to look at, and beckoning to all, and yet difficult and inspiring for the noble — for the noble nature is inspired only by what is difficult? Whatever one generation may learn from another, the properly human no generation learns from a previous one.

8.1.oldText: In this respect every generation begins primitively, has no other task than every previous generation, comes no further either, insofar as the previous generation did not betray the task and deceive itself. This properly human is passion, in which also one generation perfectly understands another and understands itself. So no generation has learned to love from another; no generation comes to begin at any other point than at the beginning; no later generation has a shorter task than the previous one; and if here one will not, like the previous generations, stop at loving, but go further — then this is only an idle and foolish talk.

8.2.oldText: But the highest passion in a human being is faith, and no generation begins here at any other point than the previous one; every generation begins from the beginning; the following generation does not get further than the previous one, insofar as that one was true to its task and did not leave it in the lurch. That this should be wearying is, of course, something the generation cannot say; for the generation, after all, has the task, and has nothing to do with the fact that the previous generation had the same task — unless the individual generation, or the individuals in the generation, presumptuously want to take the place which belongs only to the spirit that governs the world, and which has patience not to grow weary. If the generation begins on such a thing, then it is upside down; and what wonder, then, that the whole of existence seems to it upside down? For surely no one has found existence more upside down than the tailor who, according to the fairy tale, came up to heaven alive and from this standpoint regarded the world. As soon as the generation only concerns itself with its task, which is the highest, then it cannot become wearied; for the task is always sufficient for a human life. When children on a holiday have, before twelve o'clock, already played through all their games, and now impatiently say: Is there no one then who can think up a new game? — does this prove that these children are more developed and more advanced than the children in their own time or in a past generation, who could let the familiar games suffice for the whole day? Or does it not rather prove that those first children lack what I would call the lovely seriousness that belongs to play?

8.3.oldText: Faith is the highest passion in a human being. There are perhaps, in every generation, many who do not even come to it, but no one comes further. Whether also in our age there are many who do not discover it, I do not decide; I dare appeal only to myself, who do not conceal that he has long prospects ahead of him, without therefore wishing to deceive himself or the great by making this into an insignificance, into a childhood disease that one must wish to be over with as soon as possible. But also for the one who does not even come to faith, life has tasks enough, and if he loves these honestly, then his life shall not be wasted either, even if it is never like the lives of those who sensed and grasped the highest. But the one who came to faith (whether he be the eminently gifted or the simple — that makes no difference to the case), he does not stop at faith; indeed, he would be offended if anyone said it to him, just as the lover would be indignant if one said that he stopped at love; for, he would answer, by no means do I stop, since I have my life in it. Yet he does not get further either, not to anything else; for when he discovers this, then he has another explanation.

8.4.oldText: ‘One must go further; one must go further.' This urge to go further is old in the world. The dark Heraclitus, who deposited his thoughts in his writings and his writings in the temple of Diana (for his thoughts had been his armor in life, and therefore he hung it up in the temple of the god) — the dark Heraclitus said: one cannot go twice through the same

8.5.oldText: river *. The dark Heraclitus had a disciple; he did not stop here, he went further, and added: one cannot do it even once **. Poor Heraclitus, to have such a disciple! By this improvement the Heraclitean proposition was improved into an Eleatic proposition, which denies motion; and yet that disciple wished only to be a disciple of Heraclitus, who went further — not back to that which Heraclitus had left.

1.0.oldText: Ikke blot i Handelens, men ogsaa i Ideernes Verden foranstalter vor Tid ein wirklicher Ausverkauf. Alt faaes for en saadan Spot-Priis, at det bliver et Spørgsmaal, om der tilsidst er Nogen, der vil byde. Enhver spekulativ — Marqueur, der samvittighedsfuldt pointerer den nyere Philosophies betydningsfulde Gang, enhver Privatdocent, Repetent, Student, enhver Udflytter og Indsidder i Philosophien bliver ikke staaende ved at tvivle om Alt, men gaaer videre. Maaskee vilde det være utidigt og ubetimeligt at spørge dem, hvor de dog egentlig komme hen, men høfligt og beskedent er det vel at ansee det for afgjort, at de have tvivlet om Alt, da det jo ellers var en besynderlig Tale, at de gik videre. Denne foreløbige Bevægelse have de da Alle gjort og formodentlig saa let, at de ikke finde det fornødent at lade et Ord falde om, hvorledes; thi end ikke den, der ængstelig og bekymret søgte en lille Oplysning, fandt en saadan, et veiledende Vink, en lille diætetisk Forskrift om, hvorledes man forholder sig under denne uhyre Opgave. ,Men Cartesius har jo gjort det?" Cartesius, en ærværdig, ydmyg, redelig Tænker, hvis Skrifter vist Ingen kan læse uden den dybeste Rørelse, han har gjort, hvad han har sagt, og sagt, hvad han har gjort. Ak! Ak! Ak! det er en stor

1.1.oldText: Sjeldenhed i vor Tid! Cartesius har, som han selv ofte nok gjentager, ikke tvivlet i Forhold til Troen. (,Memores tamen, ut jam dictum est, huic lumint naturali tamdiu tantum esse credendum, quamdiu nihil contrarium a Deo ipso revelatur ..... Præter cætera autem, memoriæ nostræ pro summa regula est infigendum, ea quæ nobis a Deo revelata sunt, ut omnium certissima esse credenda; et quamvis forte lumen rationis, quam maxime clarum et evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videretur, soli tamen auctoritati divinæ -potius quam proprio nostro judicio fidem esse adhibendam. Cfr. Principia philosophiæ, pars prima $ 28 og $ 76). Han har ikke raabt Brand og gjort det til Pligt for Alle at tvivle, thi Cartesius var en stille eensom Tænker, ikke en brølende Gadevægter; han har beskedent bekjendt, at hans Methode kun havde Betydning for ham selv og havde " tildeels sin Grund i hans tidligere forqvaklede Viden. (Ne quis igitur putet, me hic traditurum aliquam me- - thodum, quam unusquisque sequti debeat ad recte regendam rationem; illam enim tantum, quam ipsemet secutus sum, exæponere decrevi... Sed simul ac illud studiorum curriculum absolvi (sc. juventulis, quo decurso mos est in eruditorum numerum cooptari, plane aliud coepi cogitare. Tot enim me dubiis totque erroribus implicatum esse animadverti, ut omnes discendt conatus nihil aliud mihi profuisse judicarem, quam quod ignorantiam meam magis magtisque detexissem. Cfr. Dissertatio de methodo p. 2 og 3). — Hvad hine gamle Grækere, der dog ogsaa forstode sig lidt paa Philosophien, antog at være en Opgave for hele Livet, fordi den tvivlende Færdighed ” ikke erhverves i Dage og Uger, hvad den gamle udtjente Strider opnaaede, der havde bevaret Tvivlens Ligevægt gjennem alle Besnærelser, uforfærdet negtet Sandsens Vished og Tankens Vished, ubestikkelig trodset Selvkjærlighedens Angst og Medfølelsens Insinuationer — dermed begynder i vor Tid Enhver.

1.2.oldText: I vor Tid bliver Enhver ikke staaende ved Troen, men gaaer videre. Et Spørgsmaal om, hvor de komme hen, vilde maaskee være en Dumdristighed, derimod er det vel et Tegn paa Belevenhed og Dannelse, at jeg antager, at Enhver har Troen, da det ellers bliver en besynderlige Tale: at gaae videre. I hine gamle Dage var det anderledes, da var Troen en Opgave for hele Livet, fordi man antog, at den troende Færdighed ikke erhverves hverken i Dage eller Uger. Naar da den prøvede Olding nærmede sig sit Endeligt, havde stridt den gode Strid og bevaret Troen, da var hans Hjerte ungt nok til ikke at have glemt hiin Angst og Bævelse, der tugtede Ynglingen, som Manden vel beherskede, men som intet Menneske ganske voxer fra — uden forsaavidt det skulde lykkes ved saa tidlig som mulig at gaae videre. Hvor da hine ærværdige Skikkelser naaede hen, der begynder i vor Tid Enhver for at gaae videre.

1.3.oldText: Nærværende Forfatter er ingenlunde Philosoph, han har ikke forstaaet Systemet, om det er til, om det er færdigt, han har allerede nok for sit svage Hoved i den Tanke, hvilket uhyre Hoved Enhver i vor Tid maa have, da Enhver har en saadan uhyre Tanke. Om man end var istand til at omsætte hele Troens Indhold i Begrebets Form, saa følger deraf ikke, at man har begrebet Troen, begrebet, hvorledes man kom ind i den, eller hvorledes "den kom ind i Een. Nærværende Forfatter er ingenlunde Philosoph, han er, poetice et eleganter, en Extra-Skriver, der hverken skriver Systemet eller Løfter om Systemet, der hverken forskriver sig paa Systemet. eller til Systemet. Han skriver, fordi det er ham en Luxus, der vinder i Behagelighed og Evidents, jo Færre der kjøbe og læse, hvad han skriver. Han forudseer let sin Skjæbne i en Tid, da man har slaaet en Streg over Lidenskaben for at tjene Videnskaben, i en Tid, da en Forfatter, der vil have Læsere, maa passe paa at skrive saaledes, at det beqvemt lader sig gjennemblade under Middagssøvnen, og passe paa at danne sin ydre Optræden i Lighed med hiin høflige Gartnersvends i Adresseavisen, der med Hatten i Haanden og gode Recommendationer fra det Sted, hvor han har tjent sidst, anbefaler sig til et høistæret Publikum. Han forudseer sin Skjæbne, at blive aldeles ignoreret, han aner det Forfærdelige, at den nidkjære Kritik vil lade ham flere Gange staae Skoleret; han gruer for det endnu Forfærdeligere, at en eller anden driftig Registrator, en Paragraphsluger, (der, for at frelse Videnskaben, altid er villig til at gjøre ved Andres Skrifter, hvad Trop for ,at redde Smagen" høimodigen gjorde ved »Menneskeslægtens Ødelæggelse — skal skære ham over i $8, og gjøre det med samme Ubøielighed som den Mand, der for at tjene Interpunctions-Videnskaben inddeelte sin Tale ved at tælle Ordene, saa der gik 50 Ord paa et Punktum og 35 paa et Semikolon. — Jeg falder i dybeste Underdanighed ned for enhver systematisk Posekigger: »Det er ikke Systemet, det har ikke det Mindste med Systemet at gjøre. Jeg nedbeder alt Godt over Systemet og over de danske Interessenter i denne Omnibus; thi et Taarn bliver det nok neppe. Jeg ønsker dem alle samtlige og hver især til Lykke og Velsignelse.”

2.0.oldText: Der var engang en Mand, han havde som Barn hørt hiin skjønne Fortælling om, hvorledes Gud fristede Abraham, og hvorledes han bestod i Fristelsen, bevarede Troen og anden Gang fik en Søn mod Forventning. Da han blev ældre, læste han den samme Fortælling med endnu større Beundring; thi Livet havde adskilt, hvad der var forenet i Barnets fromme Eenfoldighed. Jo ældre han blev, desto oftere vendte hans Tanke sig til hiin Fortælling, hans Begeistring blev stærkere og stærkere, og dog kunde han mindre og mindre forstaae Fortællingen. Tilsidst glemte han alt Andet over den; hans Sjæl havde kun eet Ønske, at see Abraham, een Længsel, at have været Vidne til hiin Begivenhed. Hans Begjæring var ikke at see Østerlandets skjønne Egne, ikke det forjættede Lands jordiske Herlighed, ikke hiint gudfrygtige Ægtepar, hvis Alderdom Gud velsignede, ikke den bedagede Patriarchs ærværdige Skikkelse, ikke den af Gud skjænkede Isaaks frodige Ungdom — han havde Intet mod, at det Samme foregik paa en gold Hede. Hans Attraa var at følge med de 3 Dages Reise, da Abraham reed med Sorgen foran sig og Isaak ved sin Side. Hans Ønske var at være tilstede i den Stund, da Abraham opløftede sit Øie og saae Morija-Bjerget i det Fjerne, den Stund han lod Æslerne tilbage, og gik ene med Isaak op til Bjerget; thi det, der beskjæftigede ham, var ikke Phantasiens kunstrige Væven, men Tankens Gysen.

2.1.oldText: Hiin Mand var ikke Tænker, han følte ingen Trang til at komme ud over Troen; det tyktes ham at maatte være det Herligste, at ihukommes som dens Fader, et misundelsesværdigt Lod, at eie den, om end Ingen vidste det.

2.2.oldText: Hiin Mand var ikke lærd Exeget, han kunde ikke Hebraisk; havde han kunnet Hebraisk, da havde han maaskee let forstaaet Fortællingen om Abraham.

2.3.oldText: »Og Gud fristede Abraham og sagde til ham, tag Isaak, Din eneste Søn, som Du elsker, og gaae hen i det Land Morija og offer ham der til et Brændoffer paa et Bjerg, som jeg vil vise Dig.”

2.4.oldText: Det var en aarle Morgen, Abraham stod tidlig op, han lod Æslerne sadle, forlod sit Paulun, og Isaak med ham, men Sara saae ud ad Vinduet efter dem, ned gjennem Dalen, indtil hun ikke saae dem mere. De rede tause i 3 Dage, paa den åde Dags Morgen sagde Abraham end ikke et Ord, men opløftede Øiet og saae Morija- Bjerget i det Fjerne. Han lod Drengene tilbage og gik ene med Isaak ved Haanden op til Bjerget. Men Abraham sagde til sig selv: ,jeg vil dog ikke dølge for Isaak, hvorhen denne Gang fører ham." Han stod stille, han lagde sin Haand paa Isaaks Hoved til en Velsignelse, og Isaak bøjede sig for at modtage den. Og Abrahams Aasyn var Faderlighed, hans Blik var mildt, hans Tale formanende. Men Isaak kunde ikke forstaae ham, hans Sjæl kunde ikke opløftes; han omfattede Abrahams Knæe, han bønfaldt ved hans Fod, han bad for sit unge Liv, for: sin skjønne Forhaabning, han mindede om Glæden i Abrahams Huus, han mindede om Sorgen og Eensomheden. Da reiste Abraham Drengen op og gik med ham ved sin Haand, og hans Ord vare fulde af Trøst og Formaning. Men Isaak kunde ikke forstaae ham. Han besteg Morija-Bjerget, men Isaak forstod ham ikke. Da vendte han sig bort et Øieblik fra ham, men da Isaak anden Gang saae Abrahams Aasyn, da var det forandret. hans Blik var vildt, hans Skikkelse var Rædsel. Han greb Isaak i Brystet, kastede ham til Jorden og sagde: »Dumme Dreng, troer Du jeg er Din Fader? Jeg er en Afgudsdyrker. Troer Du det er Guds Befaling? Nei det er min Lyst." Da skjælvede Isaak og raabte i sin Angst: .,Gud i Himlene forbarm Dig over mig, Abrahams Gud forbarm Dig over mig, har jeg ingen Fader paa Jorden, saa vær Du min Fader!" Men Abraham sagde sagte ved sig selv: ,Herre i Himlene, jeg takker Dig; det er dog bedre at han troer, jeg er et Umenneske, end at han skulde tabe Troen paa Dig."

2.5.oldText: Naar Barnet skal vænnes fra, da sværter Moderen sit Bryst, det var jo og Synd, at Brystet skulde see lifligt ud, naar Barnet ikke maa faae det. Saa troer Barnet, at Brystet har forandret sig, men Moderen hun er den samme, hendes Blik er kjærligt og ømt som altid. Held den, der ikke behøvede forfærdeligere Midler for at vænne Barnet fra!

2.6.oldText: Det var en aarle Morgen, Abraham stod tidlig op, han omfavnede Sara, sin Alderdoms Brud, og Sara kyssede Isaak, der tog Skændselen fra hende, hendes Stolthed, hendes Haab i alle Slægter. Såa rede de tause hen ad Veien, og Abrahams Blik var fæstet mod Jorden, til paa den åde Dag, da opløftede han Øiet og saae langt borte Morija-Bjerget, men hans Blik vendte sig atter mod Jorden. Taus lagde han Brændet til Orden, bandt Isaak, taus drog han Kniven; da saae han Væderen, som Gud havde udseet. Den offrede han og drog hjem. — — — Fra den Dag af blev Abraham gammel, han kunde ikke glemme, at Gud havde fordret det af ham. Isaak trivedes som forhen; men Abrahams Øie var fordunklet, han saae ikke Glæden mere.

2.7.oldText: Det var en aarle Morgen, Abraham stod tidlig op; han kyssede Sara, den unge Moder, og Sara kyssede Isaak, hendes Lyst, hendes Glæde i alle Tider. Og Abraham reed tankefuld hen ad Veien, han tænkte paa Hagar og Sønnen, som han jog ud i Ørkenen. Han besteg Morija-Bjerget, han drog Kniven.

2.8.oldText: Det var en stille Aften, da reed Abraham ene ud, og han reed til Morija-Bjerget; han kastede sig paa sit Aasyn, han bad Gud at tilgive ham hans Synd, at han havde villet offre Isaak, at Faderen havde glemt sin Pligt mod Sønnen. Han reed oftere sin eensomme Vei, men han havde ikke Ro. Han kunde ikke begribe, at det var en Synd, at han havde villet offre Gud det Bedste, han eiede, det, hvorfor han gjerne selv havde ladet sit Liv mange Gange; og hvis det var en Synd, hvis han ikke havde elsket Isaak saaledes, da kunde han ikke forstaae, at den kunde tilgives; thi hvilken Synd var forfærdeligere?

2.9.oldText: Det var en aarle Morgen, Alt var beredt til Reisen i Abrahams Huus. Han tog Afsked med Sara, og Elieser den troe Tjener fulgte ham ud ad Veien, indtil han atter vendte tilbage. De rede eendrægtigen sammen, Abraham og Isaak, indtil de kom til Morija-Bjerget. Men Abraham beredte Alt til Offret, rolig og mild, men idet han vendte sig bort og drog Kniven, da saae Isaak, at Abrahams Venstre knyttede sig i Fortvivlelse, at der gik en Skjælven igjennem hans Legeme — men Abraham drog Kniven.

2.10.oldText: Da vendte de atter hjem, og Sara ilede dem imøde, men Isaak havde tabt Troen. Der er i Verden aldrig sagt et Ord derom, og Isaak talte aldrig til noget Menneske, om hvad han havde seet, og Abraham anede ikke, at Nogen havde seet det.

2.11.oldText: Naar Barnet skal vænnes fra, da har Moderen den stærkere Føde ved Haanden, at Barnel ikke skal omkomme. Held den, der har den stærkere Føde ved Haanden.

2.12.oldText: Saaledes og paa mange lignende Maader tænkte hiin Mand, om hvilken vi tale, over denne Begivenhed. Hver Gang han da efter en Vandring til Morija-Bjerget vendte hjem, da sank han sammen at Træthed, han foldede sine Hænder og sagde: ,Ingen var dog stor som Abraham, hvo er istand til at forstaae ham?”

3.0.oldText: Dersom der ingen evig Bevidsthed var i et Menneske, dersom der til Grund for Alt kun laae en vildt gjærende Magt, der vridende sig i dunkle Lidenskaber frembragte Alt, hvad der var stort og hvad der var ubetydeligt, dersom en bundløs Tomhed, aldrig mættet, skjulte sig under Alt, hvad var da Livet Andet end Fortvivlelse? Dersom det forholdt sig saaledes, dersom der intet helligt Baand var, der sammenknyttede Menneskeheden, dersom den ene Slægt stod op efter den anden som Løvet i Skoven, dersom den ene Slægt afløste den anden som Fuglesangen i Skoven, dersom Slægten gik gjennem Verden, som Skibet gaaer gjennem Havet, som V. eiret gjennem Ørkenen, en tankeløs og ufrugtbar Gjerning, dersom en evig Glemsel altid hungrig lurede paa sit Bytte, og der var ingen Magt stærk nok til at frarive den det — hvor var da Livet tomt og trøstesløst! Men derfor er det ikke saaledes, og som Gud skabte Mand og Qvinde, saa dannede han Helten og Digteren eller Taleren. Denne kan Intet gjøre af hvad hiin gjør, han kan kun beundre, elske, glæde sig ved Helten. Dog er ogsaa han lykkelig, ikke mindre end denne; thi Helten er ligesom hans bedre Væsen, i hvilket han er forelsket, glad ved, at det dog ikke er ham selv, at hans Kjærlighed kan være Beundring. Han er Erindringens Genius, kan Intet gjøre uden minde om, hvad der er gjort, Intet gjøre uden beundre, hvad der er gjort; han tager Intet af sit Eget, men er misundelig paa det Betroede. Han følger sit Hjertes Valg, men naar han har fundet det Søgte, da vandrer han om for hver Mands Dør med sin Sang og med sin Tale, at Alle maae beundre Helten som han, være stolt af Helten, som han er det. Dette er hans Bedrift. hans ydmyge Gjerning, dette er hans tro Tjeneste i Heltens Huus. Bliver han saaledes sin Kjærlighed tro, strider han Dag og Nat med Glemselens Underfundighed, der vil fraliste ham Helten, da har han fuldkommet sin Gjerning, da samles han med Helten, der har elsket ham ligesaa trofast, thi Digteren er ligesom Heltens bedre Væsen, vel kraftesløs som et Minde er det, men ogsaa forklaret, som et Minde er det. Derfor skal Ingen være glemt, der var stor, og varer det end længere, tager Misforstaaelsens Sky end Helten bort, hans Elsker kommer dog, og jo længere Tiden gik hen, desto trofastere hænger han ved ham.

3.1.oldText: Nei! Ingen skal glemmes, der var stor i Verden; men Enhver var stor paa sin Viis, og Enhver i Forhold til dets Storhed, han elskede. Thi den, der elskede sig selv, blev stor ved sig selv, og den, der elskede andre Mennesker, blev stor ved sin Hengivenhed, men den, der elskede Gud, blev større end Alle. Enhver skal mindes, men Enhver blev stor i Forhold til sin Forvenftning. Een blev stor ved at forvente det Mulige; en Anden ved at forvente det Evige; men den, der forventede det Umulige, blev større end Alle. Enhver skal mindes, men Enhver var stor alt i Forhold til dets Størrelse, han stred med. Thi den, der stred med Verden, blev stor ved at overvinde Verden, og den, der stred med sig selv, blev større ved at overvinde sig selv; men den, der stred med Gud, blev større end Alle. Saaledes blev der stridt i Verden, Mand mod Mand, Fen mod

3.2.oldText: Tusinde, men den, der stred med Gud, var større end Alle. Saaledes blev der stridt paa Jorden: der var den, der overvandt Alt ved sin Kraft, og der var den, der overvandt Gud ved sin Afmagt. Der var den, der stolede paa sig selv og vandt Alt, der var den, der tryg ved sin Styrke offrede Alt, men den, der troede Gud, var større end Alle. Der var den, der var stor ved sin Kraft, og den, der var stor ved sin Viisdom, og den, der var stor ved sit Haab, og den, der var stor ved sin Kjærlighed, men Abraham var større end Alle, stor ved den Kraft, hvis Styrke er Afmagt, stor ved den Viisdom, hvis Hemmelighed er Daarskab, stor ved det Haab, hvis Form er Vanvid, stor ved den Kjærlighed, der er Had til sig selv.

3.3.oldText: Ved Troen vandrede Abraham ud fra Fædrenes Land og blev Fremmed i Forjættelsens. Han lod Eet tilbage, tog Eet med sig; han lod sin jordiske Forstand tilbage, og tog Troen med sig; ellers var han vel ikke vandret ud, men havde tænkt, det er jo urimeligt. Ved Troen var han en Fremmed i Forjættelsens Land, og der var Intet, der erindrede ham om det Kjære, men Alt fristede ved sin Nyhed hans Sjæl til veemodig Længsel. Og dog var han Guds Udvalgte, i hvem Herren havde Velbehag! Ja havde han været en Forskudt, frastødt fra Guds Naade, da kunde han bedre have fattet det, nu var det jo som en Spot over ham og over hans Tro. Der var i Verden ogsaa den, der levede forviist fra det fædrene Land, som han elskede. Han er ikke glemt, ei heller hans Klagesange, naar han i Veemod søgte og fandt det Tabte. Af Abraham er der ingen Klagesang. Det er menneskeligt at klage, menneskeligt at græde med den Grædende, men . det er større at troe, saligere at betragte den Troende. . Ved Troen modtog Abraham Forjættelsen, at i hans Sæd skulde alle Jordens Slægter velsignes. Tiden gik hen, Muligheden var der, Abraham troede; Tiden gik hen, det blev urimeligt, Abraham troede. Der var den i Verden, der ogsaa havde en Forventning. Tiden gik hen, det lakkede mod Aften, han var ikke ussel nok til at have glemt sin Forventning, derfor skal han heller ikke glemmes. Da sørgede han, og Sorgen bedrog ham ikke, som Livet havde gjort det, den gjorde for ham Alt hvad den- kunde, i i Sørgens Sødme eiede han sin skuffede Forventning. Det er menneskeligt at sørge, det er menneskeligt at sørge med den Sørgende, men det er større at troe, saligere at betragte den Troende. Af Abraham have vi ingen Sørgesang. Han talte ikke veemodig Dagene, medens Tiderne gik, han betragtede ikke Sara med mistænksomme Blikke, om hun ikke blev gammel, han standsede ikke Solens Gang, at Sara ikke skulde ældes og med hende hans Forventning, dyssende sang han ikke for Sara sit veemodige Qvad. Abrabam blev " gammel, Sara til Spot i Landet, og dog var han Guds Udvalgte og Arving til Forjættelsen, at i hans Sæd skulde alle Jordens Slægter velsignes. Saa var det jo bedre, at han ikke var Guds Udvalgte? Hvad er det at være Guds Udvalgte? Er det at blive negtet i Ungdommen Ungdommens Ønske, for med stor Besværlighed at faae det opfyldt i Alderdommen. Men Abraham troede og holdt Forjættelsen fast. Hvis Abraham havde vaklet, da havde han opgivet den. Han havde sagt til Gud: »Såaa er det dog maaskee ikke Din Villie, at det skal skee, saa vil jeg opgive Ønsket; det var mit eneste, det var min Salighed. Min Sjæl er oprigtig, jeg skjuler intet hemmeligt Nag, fordi Du negtede det.” Han skulde ikke være glemt, han skulde have frelst Mange ved sit Exempel, men dog ikke være bleven Troens Fader; thi det er stort at opgive sit Ønske, men det er større at fastholde det, efter at have opgivet det; det er stort at gribe det Evige, men det er større at fastholde det Timelige, efterat have opgivet det. — Da kom Tidens Fylde. Havde Abraham ikke troet, da var vel Sara død af Sorg, og Abraham, sløvet i Græmmelse, havde ikke forstaaet Opfyldelsen, men smilet ad den som ad en Ungdoms Drøm. Men Abraham troede, derfor var han ung; thi den, der altid haaber det Bedste, han bliver gammel, bedraget af Livet, og den, der altid er forberedt paa det Værste, han bliver tidlig gammel. men den, der troer, han bevarer en evig Ungdom. Priset derfor hiin Fortælling! Thi Sara, skjøndt alderstegen, var ung nok til at begjære Moderens Lyst, og Abraham, skjøndt graahærdet, var ung nok til at ønske at være Fader. I udvortes Henseende ligger det Vidunderlige i, at det skete efter deres Forventning, i dybere Forstand ligger Troens Vidunder i, at Abraham og Sara vare unge nok til at ønske, og at Troen havde bevaret deres Ønske og dermed deres Ungdom. Han modtog Forjættelsens Opfyldelse, han modtog den troende, og det skete efter Forjættelsen og efter Troen; thi Moses slog Klippen med sin Stav, men han troede ikke.

3.4.oldText: Da var der Glæde i Abrahams Huus, da Sara stod Brud paa Guldbryllupsdagen.

3.5.oldText: Dog saaledes skulde det ikke blive; endnu engang skulde Abraham forsøges. Han havde kæmpet med hiin snilde Magt, der opfinder Alt, med hiin aarvaagne Fjende, der aldrig blunder, med hiin gamle Mand, der overlever Alt, — han havde kæmpet med Tiden og bevaret Troen. Nu blev al Stridens Forfærdelse samlet i eet Øieblik. »Og Gud fristede Abraham og sagde til ham, tag Isaak Din eneste Søn, som Du elsker, gaa hen i det Land Morija og offer ham der til Brændoffer paa et Bjerg, som jeg vil vise Dig.”

3.6.oldText: Saa var da Alt forspildt, forfærdeligere end om det aldrig var skeet! Saa drev Herren da kun sin Spot med Abraham! Vidunderligt gjorde han det Urimelige virkeligt, nu vilde han atter see det tilintetgjort. Det var jo en Daarskab, men Abraham loe ikke deraf, som Sara, da Forjættelsen blev forkyndt. Alt var forspildt! 70 Aars trofaste Forventning, den korte Glæde ved Troens

3.7.oldText: Opfyldelse. Hvo er da den, der river Staven fra Oldingen, hvo er den, der fordrer, at han selv skal bryde den! Hvo er den, der gjør et Menneskes graae Haar trøstesløse, hvo er den, der fordrer, at han selv skal gjøre det! Er der ingen Medlidenhed med den ærværdige Olding, ingen med det uskyldige Barn! Og dog var " Abraham Guds Udvalgte, og det var Herren, der paalagde Prøvelsen. Alt skulde nu være forspildt! Slægtens herlige Ihukommelse, Forjættelsen i Abrahams Sæd, det var kun et Indfald, en flygtig Tanke, som Herren havde havt, som Abraham nu skulde udslette. Hiin herlige Skat, der var ligesaa gammel som Troen i Abrahams Hjerte, mange mange Aar ældre end Isaak, Frugten af Abrahams Liv, helliget ved Bønner, modnet i Kampe — Velsignelsen paa Abrahams Læber, denne Frugt skulde nu rives af i Utide og blive uden Betydning; thi hvad Betydning havde. den, naar Isaak skulde offres! Hiin veemodige, men dog salige Time, da Abraham skulde tage Afsked med Alt, hvad ham kjært var, da han endnu engang skulde opløfte sit ærværdige Hoved, da hans Aasyn skulde .straale som Herrens, da han skulde samle hele sin Sjæl-i en Velsignelse, der var mægtig til at gjøre Isaak velsignet alle Dage — denne Stund skulde ikke komme! Thi Afsked skulde Abraham vel tage med Isaak, men saaledes, at han selv skulde blive tilbage; Døden skulde skille dem ad, men saaledes, at Isaak blev dens Bytte. Den gamle Mand skulde ikke glad 1 Døden lægge :velsignende sin Haand paa Isaak, men træt af Livet. lægge voldsom Haand paa. Isaak. Og det var Gud, der prøvede ham. Ja Vee! Vee det Sendebud, der var kommet frem for: Abraham med en saadan .Tidende! Hvo havde vovet. at være denne Sorgens Udsending. Men det var Gud, der prøvede Abraham. …, NE |

3.8.oldText: Dog. Abraham. troede og troede for dette Liv. Ja havde hans Tro blot været for et tilkommende, da havde han vel lettere kastet Alt bort, for at haste ud af den Verden, han ikke tilhørte. Men Abrahams Tro var ikke en saadan, om der gives en saadan; thi egentlig er det ikke Tro, men Troens fjerneste Mulighed, der yderst i Synskredsen aner sin Gjenstand, dog adskilt fra den ved et svælgende Dyb, indenfor hvilket Fortvivlelsen driver sit Spil. Men Abraham troede netop for dette Liv, at han skulde blive gammel i Landet, hædret i Folket, velsignet i Slægten, uforglemmelig i Isaak, hans Kjæreste i Livet, hvem han omfattede med en Kjærlighed, for hvilken det kun var et fattigt Udtryk, at han troligen opfyldte Faderens Pligt, at elske Sønnen, som det jo og lyder med i Tilsigelsen: den Søn, som Du elsker. Jacob havde 12 Sønner og een han elskede, Abraham havde kun een, som han elskede.

3.9.oldText: Men Abraham troede og tvivlede ikke, han troede det Urimelige. Hvis Abraham havde tvivlet — da skulde han have gjort noget Andet, noget Stort og Herligt; thi hvorledes kunde Abraham gjøre Andet end hvad stort og herligt er! Han var dragen ud til Morija-Bjerget, han havde kløvet Brændet, antændt Baalet, draget Kniven — han havde raabt til Gud: ,forsmaa ikke dette Offer, det er ikke det Bedste, jeg eier, det veed jeg vel; thi hvad er en gammel Mand mod Forjættelsens Barn, men det er det Bedste, jeg kan give Dig. Lad Isaak aldrig faae det at vide, at han maa trøste sig ved sin Ungdom." Han havde stødt Kniven i sit eget Bryst. Han var bleven beundret i Verden, og hans Navn skulde ikke være glemt; men Eet er, at hlive beundret, et Andet, at blive en lededen Stjerne, der frelser den Ængstede.

3.10.oldText: Men Abraham troede. Han had ikke for sig, at han maatte bevæge Herren, det var kun da den retfærdige Straf udgik over Sodoma og Gomorra, at Abraham traadte frem med sine Bønner.

3.11.oldText: Vi læse i hine hellige Skrifter: ,0g Gud fristede Abraham, og sagde: Abraham, Abraham hvor er Du?

3.12.oldText: men Abraham svarede: her er jeg.” Du, til hvem min Tale henvender sig, var det saaledes Tilfælde med Dig? Naar Du langt borte saae de tunge Tilskikkelser nærme sig, sagde Du da ikke til Bjergene, skjuler mig, til Højene, falder over mig? Eller var Du stærkere, flyttede dog ikke Foden sig langsomt hen ad Veien, længtes den ikke ligesom tilbage efter de gamle Spor? Naar der blev kaldet ad Dig, svarede Du da, eller svarede Du ikke, maaskee sagte, og hviskende? Ikke saaledes Abraham, glad, freidig, tillidsfuld, . høit svarede han: her er jeg. Vi læse videre: ,og Abraham stod aarle om Morgenen." Som var det til en Fest, saaledes ilede han, og aarle om Morgenen var han paa det aftalte Sted, paa Morija-Bjerget. Han talte Intet til Sara, Intet til Elieser, hvo kunde ogsaa forstaa ham, havde Fristelsen ikke ved sit Væsen taget Tausheds Løfte af ham? ,Han kløvede Brændet, han bandt Isaak, han antændte Baalet, han drog Kniven." Min Tilhører! Der var mangen Fader, der troede i sit Barn at miste, hvad ham var kjærest i Verden, at berøves ethvert Fremtids Haab; men der var jo dog Ingen, der i den Forstand var Forjættelsens Barn, som Isaak var det for Abraham. Der var mangen Fader, der mistede sit Barn, men. saa var det jo Gud, den Almægtiges uforanderlige og urandsagelige Villie, hans Haand tog det. Ikke saaledes med Abraham. Ham var en tungere Prøve forbe-holdt, og Isaaks Skjæbne var med Kniven lagt i Abrahams Haand. Og han stod der, den gamle Mand med sit eneste Haab! Men han tvivlede ikke, han skuede ikke ængstelig til Højre eller Venstre, han udfordrede ikke Himlen ved sine Bønner. Han vidste, det var Gud den Almægtige, der prøvede ham, han vidste, det var det tungeste Offer, der kunde fordres af ham; men han vidste ogsaa, at intet Offer var for tungt, naar Gud fordrede det — og han drog Kniven. nl

3.13.oldText: Hvo styrkede Abrahams Arm, hvo holdt hans Høire opløftet, at den ikke. sank afmægtig ned! Den, der seer derpaa, han bliver lammet. Hvo styrkede Abrahams Sjæl, at det ikke sortnede for hans Øie, saa han hverken saae Isaak eller Væderen! Den, der seer derpaa, han bliver blind. — Og dog sjelden nok er maaskee. den, der bliver lam og blind, endnu sjednere den, der værdigen fortæller, hvad der skete. Vi vide det Alle — det var kun en Prøvelse.

3.14.oldText: Hvis Abraham, da han stod paa Morija-Bjerget, havde tvivlet, hvis han raadvild havde skuet omkring sig, hvis han, inden han drog Kniven, ved et Tilfælde havde opdaget Væderen, hvis Gud havde tilladt ham at offre den istedenfor Isaak — da var han dragen hjem, Alt var det Samme, han havde Sara, han beholdt Isaak, og dog hvor forandret! Thi hans Tilbagetog var en Flugt, hans Frelse et Tilfælde, hans Løn Beskæmmelse, hans Fremtid. maaskee Fortabelse. Da havde han - hverken vidnet om sin Tro eller om Guds Naade, men vidnet om, hvor forfærdeligt det er, at drage op til Morija-Bjerget. Da skulde Abraham ikke være glemt, ei heller Morija-Bjerget. Dette skulde da nævnes ikke som Årarat, hvor Arken landede, men nævnes. som en Forfærdelse, fordi det var her, at Abraham tvivlede.

3.15.oldText: Ærværdige Fader Abraham! Da. Du drog hjem fra Morija-Bjerget, da behøvede Du ingen Lovtale, der kunde trøste Dig for det Tabte; thi Du vandt jo Alt, og beholdt Isaak, var det ikke saaledes? Herren . tog ham ikke mere fra Dig, men Du sad. glad tilbords med ham i Dit Paulun, som Du hisset gjør det i alle Evigheder. Ærværdige Fader Abraham! Aartusinder ere henrundne siden hine Dage, men Du behøver ingen sildig Elsker, der kan udrive Dit Minde af Glemsels Vold; thi ethvert Tungemaal minder Dig — og dog lønner Du Din Elsker herligere end Nogen, Du gjør ham hisset salig i Dit

3.16.oldText: Skjød, Du fængsler her hans Øie og hans Hjerte ved Din Gjernings Vidunderlighed. Ærværdige Fader Abraham! Slægtens anden Fader! Du, der først forhnam og vidnede om hiin uhyre Lidenskab, der forsmaaer den forfærdelige Kamp med Elementers Rasen og Skabningens Kræfter for at stride med Gud, Du, der først kjendte hiin højeste Lidenskab, det hellige, rene, ydmyge Udtryk for det guddommelige Vanvid, der blev beundret af Hedninger — tilgiv den, der vilde tale til Din Priis, om han ikke gjorde det retteligen. Han talede ydmygt, som det var hans Hjertes Begjæring, han talede kort, som det sømmer sig, men han skal aldrig glemme, at Du behøvede 100 Aar for at faae en Alderdoms Søn mod Forventning, at Du maatte drage Kniven, før Du beholdt Isaak, han skal aldrig glemme, at Du i 130 Aar ikke kom videre end til Troen.

4.0.oldText: Et gammelt Ord, hentet fra den udvortes og synlige Vreden, siger: ,kun den, der arbeider, faaer Brødet.” Besynderligt nok, Ordet passer ikke paa den Verden, hvor den nærmest har hjemme; thi den udvortes Verden er Ufuldkommenhedens Lov underlagt, og her gjentager det sig atter og atter, at ogsaa den, der ikke arbeider, faaer Brødet, at den, der sover, faaer det rigeligere, end den, der arbeider. I den udvortes Verden er Alt Ihændehaverens; den træller under Ligegyldighedens Lov, og den, der har Ringen, ham lyder Ringens Aand, enten han er en Noureddin eller en Aladdin, og den, der har Verdens Skatte, han har dem, hvorledes han end fik dem. I Aandens Verden er det anderledes. Her hersker en evig guddommelig Orden, her regner det ikke baade over Retfærdige og Uretfærdige. her skinner Solen ikke baade over Gode og Onde, her gjælder det, at kun den, der arbeider, faaer Brødet, kun den, der var i Angst, finder Hvile, kun den, der stiger ned i Underverdenen, frelser den Elskede, kun den, der drager Kniven, faaer Isaak. Den, der ikke vil arbeide, han faaer ikke Brødet, men bliver bedragen, som Guderne bedrog Orpheus med en luftig Skikkelse istedenfor den Elskede, bedrog ham, fordi han var kjelen, ikke modig, bedrog ham, fordi han var Cilharspiller, ikke Mand. Her hjælper det ikke at have Abraham til Fader, eller 17 Ahner, den, der ikke vil arbeide, ham passer det paa, hvad der staaer skrevet om Israels Jomfruer, han føder Vind, men den, der vil arbeide, han føder sin egen Fader.

4.1.oldText: Der er en Viden, der formastelig vil indføre i Aandens Verden den samme Ligegyldighedens Lov, som den, under hvilken den udvortes Verden sukker. Den mener, at det er nok at vide det Store, andet Arbeide behøves der ikke. Men derfor faaer den ikke Brødet, den omkommer af Hunger, medens Alt forvandler sig til Guld. Og hvad veed den ogsaa? Der var mange Tusinder i den græske Samtid, utallige i de senere Slægter, der vidste alle Miltiades's Triumpher, men der var kun Een, der blev søvnløs over dem. Der var talløse Slægter, der vidste Ord til andet udenad Fortællingen om Abraham, hvor Mange gjorde den søvnløs?

4.2.oldText: Fortællingen om Abraham har nu den mærkelige Egenskab, at den altid bliver herlig, hvor fattigt man end forstaaer den, men dog gjælder det atter her, om man vil arbeide og være besværet. Men arbeide vil man ikke, og dog vil man forstaae Fortællingen. Man taler til Abrahams Ære, men hvorledes? Man giver det Hele et ganske almindeligt Udtryk: ,det var det Store, at han elskede Gud saaledes, at han vilde offre ham det Bedste." Det er meget sandt; men det , Bedste" er et ubestemt Udtryk. Man identificerer i Tankens og Mundens Løb ganske trygt Isaak og det Bedste, og den Mediterende kan godt ryge sin Pibe under Meditationen, og den Hørende kan godt strække Benene mageligt ud fra sig. Dersom hiin rige Yngling, hvem Christus mødte paa sin Vei, havde solgt alt sit Gods og givet det til de Fattige, da skulde vi prise ham, som alt hvad der er Stort, og end ikke forstaae ham uden at arbeide, men han var dog ikke bleven en Abraham, uagtet han offrede det Bedste. Det man udelader af Abrahams Historie er Angesten; thi mod Penge har jeg ingen ethisk Forpligtelse, men mod Sønnen har Faderen den høieste og helligste. Dog Angest er en farlig Sag for Blødagtige, derfor glemmer man den, og desuagtet vil man tale om Abraham. Man taler da, i Talens Løb vexle de tvende Udtryk: Isaak og det Bedste, Alt gaaer ypperligt. Traf det sig imidlertid saa, at der iblandt Tilhørerne var en Mand, der leed af Søvnløshed, da ligger den forfærdeligste, den dybeste, tragiske og comiske Misforstaaelse meget nær. Han gik hjem, han vilde gjøre ligesom Abraham; thi Sønnen er jo det Bedste. Hvis hiin Taler fik det at vide, da gik han maaskee til ham, han samlede al sin geistlige Værdighed og raabte: ,afskyelige Menneske, Udskud af Samfundet, hvilken Djævel har saaledes besat Dig, at Du vil myrde Diu Søn.” Og Præsten, som ikke havde sporet nogen Varme eller Transpiration ved at prædike om Abraham, han forbausedes over sig selv, over den Alvorens Vrede, med hvilken han nedtordnede hiint stakkels Menneske; han var glad over sig selv; thi han havde aldrig talet med saadan Fynd og Salvelse; han sagde til sig selv og sin Kone: ,Jeg er Taler, det, der har manglet, har været Anledningen, da jeg i Søndags talte om Abraham, følte jeg mig aldeles ikke greben."” 0Dersom samme Taler havde en lille Overflødighed af Forstand, der lod sig tabe, saa tænker jeg han tabte den, hvis Synderen roligt og værdigt svarede: det var jo, hvad Du selv prædikede om i Søndags. Hvorledes skulde ogsaa Præsten kunne faae Sligt i sit Hoved, og dog var det jo saa, og Feilen kun den, at han ikke havde vidst, hvad han sagde. At der dog ikke er en Digter. der kunde beslutte sig til at foretrække saadanne Situationer for det Fias og Tant, hvormed man fylder Comedier og Romaner! Det Comiske og det Tragiske berøre her hinanden i absolut Uendelighed. sPræstens Tale var maaskee i og for sig latterlig nok, men blev uendelig latterlig ved sin Virkning, og dog var define ganske naturlig. Eller hvis Synderen virkelig uden at gjøre nogen Indvending blev omvendt af Præstens Straffetale, hvis denne nidkjære Geistlige gik glad hjem, glad i Bevidstheden om, at han ikke blot virkede fra Prædikestolen, men fremfor Alt med uimodstaaelig Magt som Sjælesørger, idet han om Søndagen begeistrede Menigheden, medens han om Mandagen som en Cherub med luende Glavind stillede sig for den, der ved sin Gjerning vilde gjøre hiint gamle Ord til Skamme, at det ikke gaaer til i Verden som Præsten prædiker ”).

4.3.oldText: Hvis Synderen derimod ikke blev overbeviist, saa er hans Situation tragisk nok. Han blev da formodentlig henrettet eller sendt i Daarekisten, kort, han blev ulykkelig i Forhold til den saakaldte Virkelighed, i en anden Forstand tænker jeg vel, at Abraham gjorde ham lykkelig; thi den, der arbeider, omkommer ikke.

4.4.oldText: Hvoraf forklarer man en saadan Modsigelse som hiin Talers? Er det fordi Abraham har faaet Hævd paa et være en stor Mand, saa at hvad han gjør, er stort, og naar en Anden gjør det Samme, er det Synd, himmelraabende Synd? I saa Fald da ønsker jeg ikke at deeltage i slig tankeløs Lovprisen. Kan Troen ikke gjøre det til en hellig Handling at ville myrde sin Søn, saa lad den samme Dom gaae over Abraham som over enhver Anden. Mangler man maaskee Mod til at gjennemføre sin Tanke, at sige, at Abraham var en Morder, da er det vel bedre at erhverve dette Mod, end at spilde Tiden paa ufortjente Lovtaler. Det ethiske Udtryk for hvad Abraham gjorde er, at han vilde myrde Isaak, det t( I gamle Dage sagde man: det er sørgeligt, at det ikke gaaer til i Verden som Præsten prædiker — maaskee kommer den Tid, især ved Philosophbiens Hjælp, da man kan sige: heldigviis gaaer det ikke saaledes til som Præsten prædiker; thi i Livet er der dog lidt Mening, i hans Præken er der slet ingen.

4.5.oldText: religieuse er, at han vilde offre Isaak; men i denne Modsigelse ligger netop Angesten, der vel kan gjøre et Menneske søvnløst, og dog er Abraham ikke den, han er, uden denne Angst. Eller gjorde Abraham maaskee slet ikke, hvad der fortælles, var det maaskee paa Grund af hine Tiders Forhold noget ganske Andet, saa lad os glemme ham; thi hvad er det Umagen værd at erindre det Forbigangne, der ikke kan blive et Nærværende. Eller bavde maaskee hiin Taler glemt Noget, der svarede til den ethiske Forglemmelse, at Isaak var Sønnen. Naar Troen nemlig ved at blive til Nul og Nichts tages bort, saa bliver kun det raae Factum tilbage, at Abraham vilde myrde Isaak, hvilket er nemt nok at eftergjøre for Enhver, der ikke har Troen, det vil sige den Tro, der gjør ham det svært.

4.6.oldText: Jeg for mit Vedkommende mangler ikke Mod til at tænke en Tanke heel; hidtil har jeg ingen frygtet, skulde jeg støde paa en saadan, da vil jeg haabe, at jeg idetmindste har Oprigtighed til at sige, denne Tanke frygter jeg, den oprører noget Andet i mig og derfor vil jeg ikke tænke den, gjør jeg Uret dermed, saa vil Straffen vel ikke udeblive. Hvis jeg havde erkjendt det for Sandhedens Dom, at Abraham var en Morder, da veed jeg ikke, om jeg havde kunnet bringe min Pietet for ham til Taushed. Havde jeg imidlertid lænkt det, saa havde jeg formodentlig tiet dermed; thi i slige Tanker skal man ikke indvie Andre. Men Abraham er intet Blendværk, han har ikke sovet sig til sin Navnkundighed, han skylder den ikke en Lune af Skjæbnen.

4.7.oldText: Kan man da uforbeholdent tale om Abraham, uden at løbe Fare for, at en Enkelt gaaer hen i Forvildelse og gjør ligesaa? Tør jeg det ikke, saa vil jeg reent tie om Abraham, og fremfor Alt vil jeg ikke nedsætte ham saaledes, at han netop derved bliver en Snare for de Svage. Gjør man nemlig Troen til Alt a: til det, den er, saa tænker jeg vel, man tør tale uden Fare derom i vor Tid, der neppe extravagerer i Troen, og det er kun ved Troen man faaer Lighed med Abraham, ikke ved Mordet. Gjør man Kjærligheden til en flygtig Stemning, en vellystig Rørelse i et Menneske, saa lægger man kun Snarer for den Svage, naar man vil tale om Kjærlighedens Bedrifter. En forbigaaende Bevægelse har vel Enhver, men hvis derfor Enhver vilde gjøre det Forfærdelige, som Kjærligheder har helliget som udødelig Bedrift, da er Alt tabt, baade Bedriften og den Forvildede. Der lod sig da vel tale om Abraham; thi det Store kan aldrig skade, naar det opfattes i sin Storhed; det er som et tveægget Sværd, der dræber og frelser. Hvis Loddet faldt paa mig at tale derom, da vilde jeg begynde med at vise, hvilken from og gudfrygtig Mand Abraham var, værdig at kaldes Guds Udvalgte. Kun en Saadan paalægges en saadan Prøve; men hvo er en Saadan? Dernæst vilde jeg skildre, hvorledes Abraham elskede. Isaak. Til den Ende vilde jeg bede alle gode Aander staae mig bi, at min Tale maatte blive glødende som Faderkjærligheden er det. Jeg haaber da at skulle skildre den saaledes, at der ikke blev mangen Fader i Kongens Riger og Lande, der turde paastaae, at han elskede saaledes. Men elskede han ikke som Abraham, saa var jo enhver Tanke om at offre Isaak en Anfægtelse. Dette kunde man allerede tale adskillige Søndage om, man behøver jo ikke at forhaste sig. Følgen vilde da blive, hvis der blev talet retteligen, at en Deel Fædre . slet ikke vilde forlange at høre mere, men indtil videre være glade ved, om det virkelig lykkedes dem at elske saaledes, som Abraham elskede. Var der da Een, som, efter at have hørt det Store, men ogsaa det Forfærdelige i Abrahams Daad, vovede at gaae frem ad Veien; da vilde jeg sadle min Hest og ride med ham. Paa hver Station, indtil vi kom til Morija-Bjerget, vilde jeg forklare ham, at han endnu kunde vende om, kunde angre den Misforstaaelse, at han var kaldet til at forsøges i saadan Strid, kunde bekjende, at han manglede Mod, saa Gud selv maatte tage Isaak, hvis han vilde have ham. Det er min Overbeviisning, at et saadant Menneske ikke er forskudt, at han kan blive salig med alle Andre, men i Tiden bliver han det ikke. Vilde man, selv i de mest troende Tider, ikke dømme saaledes om et saadant Menneske? jeg har kjendt et Menneske, der engang kunde have frelst mit Liv, hvis han havde været højimodig. Han | sagde ligefrem: ,jeg seer nok, hvad jeg kunde gjøre; men jeg vover det ikke, jeg frygter, at jeg senere skal mangle Kraft, at jeg skal fortryde det.” Han var ikke høimodig, men hvo vilde dog derfor ikke vedblive at elske ham?

4.8.oldText: Naar jeg da saaledes havde talt, havde bevæget Tilhørerne, saa de dog havde fornummet Troens dialektiske Kampe og dens gigantiske Lidenskab, da vilde jeg ikke forskylde en Vildfarelse fra de Tilhørendes Side, at de skulde tænke: ,han har nu Troen i saa høi en Grad, os er det allerede nok, at holde i Skjøderne paa ham.” Jeg. vilde nemlig tilføje: ,jeg har ingenlunde Troen. Jeg er af Naturen et kløgtigt Hoved og ethvert saadant

4.11.oldText: Kjærligheden har dog i Digterne sine Præster, og stundom hører man en Røst, der veed at holde den i Hævd; men om Troen høres der intet Ord, hvo taler til denne Lidenskabs Ære? Philosophien gaaer videre. Theologien sidder sminket ved Vinduet og beiler til dens Gunst, falbyder sin Deilighed til Philosophien. Jeg for mit Vedkommende har 3?

4.12.oldText: anvendt adskillig Tid paa at forstaae den hegelske Philosophi, troer ogsaa nogenlunde at have forstaaet den, er dumdristig nok til at mene, at, naar jeg, trods anvendt Umage, paa enkelte Steder ikke kan forstaae ham, saa har han nok ikke selv været ganske klar. Alt Dette gjør jeg let, naturligt, mit Hoved lider ikke derved. Naar jeg derimod skal til at tænke over Abraham, da er jeg som tilintetgjort. Jeg faaer i ethvert Moment Øie paa hiint uhyre Paradox, der er Indholdet af Abrahams Liv, i ethvert Moment bliver jeg stødt tilbage, og min Tanke kan, trods al sin Lidenskab, ikke trænge ind i det, ikke komme et Haarsbred videre.
